text:
An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


44
Feedback to Proposed decision CRU202504
In the feedback to the proposed decision some respondents proposed distinguishing
between hyperscale, wholesale, and retail data centres within this policy. Some respondents
described the impacts of the different data centre types and differences between these. It
was described that hyperscale self-build represents three-quarters of the existing data centre
footprint in Ireland in terms of capacity (MW). Over half of Ireland’s operational data centres
have IT capacity below 10 MW, with these data centres constituting less than 18% of the
total MIC power capacity of all operational data centres in Ireland. Data centres with capacity
above 10 MW IT are contracted for 82% of data centre MIC capacity on the national
electricity network. Some respondents suggested including exemptions or less stringent
requirements for smaller facilities (lower MIC) to avoid stifling growth and innovation. Some
respondents suggested that requirements for dispatchable generation in the SEM from smaller
data centres were unreasonable. Some respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504
suggested alternative approaches to requiring generation that participates in the SEM to
ensure flexibility and reduce onerous requirements. These respondents suggested allowing
non-market-integrated on-site generation, to reduce barriers while ensuring system flexibility
and reliability.
Treatment of smaller data centres
The CRU notes there may be some merit in having different requirements for smaller data
centres versus requirements placed on larger data centres, which still meet the overall
requirements of this policy. For example, for a demand connection below a certain scale it may
be proportionately more onerous to require a separate connection and metering for any
required generation and/or storage. However, the CRU sees merit in leveraging the existing
scheduling and dispatch, and settlement systems used in the SEM. This may justify using a
market unit in the SEM which would facilitate behind the meter arrangements, such as an
autoproducer unit that can be traded and dispatched through the SEM. As part of the
engagement process on this policy, a concern raised by ESB Networks was the additional use
of substation equipment that would be required for separate connections for demand and
generation. This may also contribute towards justification for different requirements for smaller
data centres below a certain size.
In order to meet the overall requirements of this policy and to acknowledge the distinction
between larger and smaller data centre sites, the CRU sees merit in requiring smaller data
centres to support the system with behind the meter services in the form of an autoproducer

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


45
which participates in the wholesale electricity market (SEM). The CRU favours a centrally
dispatched approach for this requirement which will help facilitate the optimum solution on a
system-wide operational basis where possible via existing market structures. This will help the
system to make efficient use of available renewable electricity on the system. The CRU
considers that it is necessary for these services to be provided through the SEM to assist in
ensuring the continuity, security, and quality of supply of electricity is maintained. These
arrangements would allow these sites to develop and engineer solutions behind the meter
which support the system and are on the same electrical line as the demand. The CRU notes
that the demand site would benefit from avoided network charges and energy payments based
on the net energy position of the site. This may have an impact on the amount these sites
contribute to support the system and on the overall charging base. While the requirement for
the generation to be registered and dispatched through the market is expected to reduce the
impact of these arrangements on the overall tariff charging base, the CRU considers that there
should be a threshold below which these arrangements are considered appropriate to further
limit the impact. In the CRU’s view the threshold should be for applicants seeking an MIC
equal to or above the de-minimis level (1MVA) and below 10MVA. The requirements on data
centres captured in this category would be distinct to those described in sub section “3.4
Requirement for all data centres equal to or above 10 MVA”.
Approach for data centres with MIC ≥ de-minimis level & < 10MVA
Data centre connection applications equal to or above the de-minimis level (1MVA) and with
an MIC <10MVA will be required to provide an autoproducer in the SEM which matches 100%
of the demand site’s MIC on a de-rated basis (reflecting the underlying technology), facilitated
through assets situated behind the demand site’s meter. The data centre, acting as an
autoproducer, would be required to set up as a trading site in the SEM. This autoproducer
would need to be able to run on an operational basis e.g. not be bound by limited run hours
outside of agreed levels of routine necessary maintenance. The de-rated capacity of the
autoproducer unit must at a minimum meet the site’s MIC for the duration of the data centre
demand connection and be operational. In the CRU’s view the autoproducer should have to
meet some minimum performance and availability requirements. This new capacity should
be made available to the system on an operational basis in order to reflect the additional
demand capacity of the data centre and support the continuity, security, and quality of supply
of electricity for the wider system. As described in Section 3.9.3 Connection process and
assessment the CRU requires the electrical SOs to each publish an engagement and
connection process for data centre connection applicants by 31 March 2026. As part of this
process the SOs will outline minimum expected performance and availability requirements

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


46
for autoproducer units. In relation to the performance and availability of the autoproducer
unit, it is envisaged that reliability of service will be a contractual requirement for the data
centre demand connection. If the performance and availability of the autoproducer site falls
below this minimum expected reliability or provision of available capacity to the system, the
SOs will have the ability to reduce the MIC of the related data centre’s demand connection.
This should be set out by the SOs within contractual arrangements. The CRU is of the view
that the provision of an autoproducer in the SEM which is compliant in meeting 100% of the
demand site’s MIC on a de-rated basis as described in this section removes the need for
additional Mandatory Demand Curtailment (MDC) measures.
Participation of the autoproducer in the SEM leverages the existing market settlement
systems, providing a participant with remuneration from the wholesale electricity markets for
providing these services to the system. Any autoproducer units developed by data centres
under this approach would participate through the existing market structures, contributing to
price formation in these different markets. Excluding assets of this scale (and possibly multiple
sites) from the existing market structures could distort the operation of the wholesale market.
Acknowledgement of renewables contribution
Section 3.5 Renewable Electricity Requirement sets out a new requirement that at least 80%
of annual demand annual should be met with renewable electricity generated in the Republic
of Ireland.  The CRU is of the view that renewable generation contracted to provide up to 80%
of annual demand should be taken into account when determining the requirement for
autoproducer unit in the SEM (e.g. meeting the MIC on de-rated basis). This associated
renewable generation can be reflected on a de-rated basis against the de-rated autoproducer
requirement. The de-rating to be applied for the purposes of connection requirements will be
informed by the de-rating curves that are published in most recent CRM T-4 capacity auction
information packs as part of the CRM auctions in the wholesale electricity market (SEM). The
de-rating information to be used to inform the sizing of the generation in the autoproducer unit
in relation to the sites MIC will be the most recent available at the time of the planning
submission.
Other considerations
The CRU considers that there may be cases where multiple data centres with an MIC of less
than 10MVA may seek to join together to develop a single shared generator and or storage
facility. Equally a single data centre with an MIC of less than 10MVA may seek to develop a
separately connected proximate generator and or storage facility. Insofar as the proximate

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


47
generation and/or storage is able to comply with the requirements as set out in Section 3.4
and meets the combined MIC of the data centre(s) on a de-rated basis, then these
approaches could be deemed acceptable. The CRU notes that there may be local system
reasons why the relevant SO would not be able to accommodate these configurations for
generation and/or storage as a solution or where alternative connection arrangements may be
required. This assessment would be done on a case-by-case basis by the relevant SO.
The CRU notes that any potential behaviour by applicants such as ‘project splitting’ in order to
fit a larger project into this smaller data centre category is not appropriate. The CRU notes that
the MIC <10MVA threshold is based on the size of the whole project. Multiple applications
below the threshold level (<10MVA) for the same project will not be permitted and the
requirements of this policy must be considered on an aggregated basis in such scenarios. Any
behaviour which is considered by System Operator(s) to have the effect of separating a project
into multiple applications in order to qualify under the threshold level (<10MVA) will not be
deemed acceptable, as this would undermine this policy and potentially increase security of
supply risks. The CRU may review these requirements going forward in light of performance of
the above arrangements and new developments in the evolution of the network.

Decision
The Commission has made a decision that data centres which are above the de-minimis
level (1MVA) and have an MIC <10MVA are required to provide an autoproducer unit that
meets 100% of the demand site’s MIC on de-rated basis which participates in the SEM.
The Commission has made a decision that the associated renewable generation contribution
(up to 80% of annual demand) should be acknowledged and can be reflected on a de-rated
basis against the autoproducer requirement (see Section 3.5 Renewable Electricity
Requirement).
The Commission has made a decision that any data centres which are equal to or above the
de-minimis level (1MVA) and have an MIC <10MVA and compliant in providing autoproducer
unit as required under this decision will not be required to meet MDC provisions.
The Commission has made a decision that, for any data centres which are equal to or above
the de-minimis level (1MVA) and have an MIC <10MVA, the de-rated capacity of the
autoproducer unit must at a minimum meet the site’s MIC for the duration of the connection
and be operational.

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


48
3.4. Requirements for all data centres equal to or above 10
MVA
The CRU is of the view that data centre connection applications seeking a Maximum Import
Capacity (MIC) of 10MVA and above should be required to provide onsite or proximate
generation and/or storage with a Maximum Export Capacity (MEC) which is equal to or greater
than their MIC (subject to derating requirements), with this generation being separately
connected and metered, and required to participate in the wholesale electricity market. Also
depending on the size of the site’s MIC, an applicant may choose, or it may be required by the
relevant SO, that this generation is provided in the form of a number of separate dispatchable
generator units. As described in Proposed Decision CRU202504 the scale and speed of new
data centre demand presents an infrastructure development timing challenge, with the
potential for this significant new demand to connect faster than the required generation
capacity or network capacity can be delivered. Requiring a data centre to provide onsite or
proximate generation and/or storage which participates in the wholesale markets would ensure
that the additional operational electricity needs of the demand site are catered for through the
market while maintaining the continuity, security, and quality of supply of electricity for the
wider system. The CRU notes that data centre demand sites may develop the generation
assets directly or may choose to contract with service providers to meet these requirements.

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


49
3.4.1. Separate connection and metering
The CRU is of the view that data centres with MIC equal to or greater than 10MVA should be
required to provide onsite or proximate generation and/or storage which is connected
separately and metered separately to the data centre demand connection. In feedback to
Proposed Decision CRU202504 some respondents supported the requirement for
onsite/proximate generation to be independently connected to the grid, with this seen as
beneficial for ensuring system reliability and optimising the use of dispatchable energy plants.
Other respondents raised concerns about the practicality and economic viability of separate
connections for onsite/proximate generation. One respondent highlighted the need for
significant infrastructure investment due to the requirement for a separate grid connection for
each generator, resulting in increased capital expenditure for data centres and grid operators.
One respondent was of the view that this setup introduces inefficiencies in energy use, as
power generated on-site must first be exported to the grid before it can be consumed by the
data centre, causing unnecessary transmission and/or distribution losses. This respondent
suggested that a more technically and economically efficient approach would be to integrate
onsite generation directly with LEU demand.
The CRU considers the requirement for data centres to provide onsite or proximate generation
and/or storage which is separately connected and metered to be the optimum approach for the
system, supporting security of supply. By requiring a separate connection point, the SO has
full visibility of the generation unit which can provide system services such as operating
reserve and reactive power without impacting the operation of the demand unit. The required
onsite or proximate generation and/or storage will be connected separately and centrally
dispatched similar to any other generator in the SEM serving the energy needs of the overall
system and not just the specific data centre site, enabling the optimum use of generation for
the overall system on an ongoing basis. All electricity market charges and a significant
percentage of electricity network charges are levied on SEM demand on a €/MWh basis. In
this approach all of the data centres energy volume would face these network charges, helping
to support the system. The CRU notes similar considerations by authorities in other markets
such as in North America14.

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


50
3.4.2. Definition of proximate generation and/or storage
As proposed in CRU202504 the CRU considers that connection applicants should have the
flexibility to request the siting of this generation and/or storage either onsite or proximate to the
site of their data centre (i.e. connected to the Transmission or Distribution system close to the
demand connection). Many respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 emphasised the
need for a clear and precise definition of the term 'proximate generation'. Some respondents
suggested defining it as either geographically or electrically proximate. Suggestions included
defining it as assets connected at the same electrical node or within a specific radius. It was
suggested the lack of clarity had caused confusion among stakeholders. Some respondents
expressed concerns about the feasibility of meeting proximate generation requirements due
to planning, financial, and logistical challenges.
The use of proximate generation and/or storage aims to address challenges in
accommodating this generation and reflects how it may be challenging in certain space
constrained locations to accommodate generation onsite, and provides the ability to locate the
generation on another site that may be more suitable. The ability to use proximate rather than
only onsite generation may facilitate innovative solutions, for example allowing multiple data
centres to develop a single larger proximate generator to cover their collective MIC. The
System Operators will be empowered to decide on whether the proposed siting of generation
assets meets the required system needs. In the CRU’s view this proximate generation would
need to be electrically close at a minimum. The CRU does not see merit in defining proximate
on a geographic basis, as this may not accurately reflect the level of electrical interconnection
between a data centre demand site and proposed generation and/or storage asset(s). In the
first instance, applicants should seek to propose generation at the same node as a proposed
data centre demand connection, however, where this is not feasible, the applicant could
propose other options to the SOs for consideration. Assessment of proposals from applicants
would be done on a case-by-case basis by the relevant SO. The CRU notes that there may
be local system reasons why the relevant SO would not be in a position to accommodate
proximate generation as a solution. The requirement to bring onsite or proximate generation
is primarily to address risks around generation adequacy and security of supply and will be
subject to the relevant application process, e.g. ECP-GSS, in the same manner as other
generation applying for a grid connection.
3.4.3. Participation in wholesale electricity market
The CRU has determined that a data centre connection application seeking 10MVA or above
will be required to provide onsite or proximate generation and/or storage, that will participate

text:
An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


51
in the wholesale electricity market (Single Electricity Market) as a standalone generator
separately connected and metered. As this dispatchable generation and/or storage is
>10MVA, under current market arrangements it is required to participate in the energy and
capacity markets (existing dispatchable generators) e.g. Balancing Market, Capacity
Remuneration Mechanism (CRM) and being subject to market rules such as the Trading &
Settlement Code, the Bidding Code of Practice and the Capacity Market Code.
Some respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 expressed concerns about the
requirement for data centres to participate in the SEM. Some respondents suggested that
SEM participation introduces significant financial and logistical burdens, potentially
undermining the business case for data centres. Concerns raised included the need for
major capital expenditures and the risk of unintended consequences in the market. Some
respondents argued that mandatory participation may render projects commercially unviable
and misaligned with long-term energy strategies. There were suggestions that this
requirement may deter investment and alternative approaches to ensure flexibility and
reduce burdens were proposed. Some respondents suggested allowing non-market-
integrated on-site generation, to reduce barriers while ensuring system flexibility and
reliability. Concerns were expressed about the mandatory requirement for data centres to
participate in the capacity market, citing increased complexity, cost, and planning
challenges. Some respondents emphasised the need for clarity on how CRM participation
integrates with planning frameworks, grid codes, and regulatory processes.
The CRU considers that it is necessary and proportionate to require new data centres to
provide onsite or proximate generation and/or storage that will participate in the wholesale
electricity market. This is to assist in ensuring the continuity, security, and quality of supply of
electricity is maintained. In the absence of these measures being implemented, the addition
of new data centre demand could mean system security standards being threatened. The
CRU favours a centrally dispatched approach for this requirement which will help facilitate
the optimum solution on a whole system operational basis where possible via existing
market structures. This will help the system to efficiently use available renewable electricity
on the system. This approach will require a new data centre providing 100% operational
capacity to a level equal to or greater than their sites MIC (on de-rated basis) and
participation of this generation in the wholesale electricity market. This requirement does not
specify the generation and/or storage technology or fuel used. The CRU notes that data
centre demand sites may develop the generation assets directly or may choose to contract
with service providers to meet these requirements.

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


52
Participation in the SEM leverages the existing market settlement systems, providing a
participant with potential for remuneration from the wholesale electricity markets for
providing these services to the system. Any new generation and/or storage assets
developed by data centres under this approach would participate through the existing market
structures, contributing to price formation in these different markets. Excluding these new
generation and/or storage assets of this scale from the existing market structures could
distort the operation of the wholesale market.
3.4.4. Interaction with CRM
In relation to the capacity auction some respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504
requested detailed guidance on the capacity allocation, and sought clarity on the effect the
entry of new demand may have on the capacity auction demand curve. The Capacity Market
is designed to help ensure that the generation capacity in the SEM is sufficient to meet
demand and that requirements relating to generation adequacy are satisfied. The demand
curve reflects the amount of generation that needs to be procured in a given auction.
Capacity auctions are run annually to procure generation capacity for delivery in 4 years (T-
4) and for delivery in 1 year (T-1). The CRU notes concerns raised as to the potential
scenario of existing generation units being displaced, unintentionally distorting the auction
outcome due to a disconnect in timing between new data centre demand and its related
generation and/or storage being reflected in the demand curve15.
In the current capacity mechanism auction arrangements, all of the new generation capacity
may be reflected in a relevant T-4 CRM auction for a delivery year. Meanwhile the
corresponding data centre demand may be projected to ramp up over a number of years
(e.g. 20%, 40%, 60% of final demand) to an assumed enduring utilisation rate (e.g. 80%). In
a scenario where this were not mitigated, this could create a temporal mismatch between the
generation and demand volumes during a number of auction delivery years. This is
Illustrated in Figure 8 below.


15 SEMO – June 2025 - CRM T-4 2029/2030 Capacity Auction Parameters consultation includes
parameters for the demand curve for 2029/2030 – link here

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


53

Figure 8: Indicative graph showing potential mismatch between data centre demand and generation in CRM auctions

Another possible issue that the CRU has considered relates to a scenario whereby a
generator linked to new data centre demand is successful in the T-4 capacity auction (CRM),
securing a 10-year fixed price contract. Consideration was given to a scenario where the
new data centre demand does not materialise as expected or exits the market prematurely
(before the 10-year fixed price contract from CRM has finished). This could risk leaving the
cost/exposure of this contracted capacity to be covered by other electricity demand users for
the remaining period left in the CRM contract. Given the potential scale of demand and
related generation associated with data centres, this could represent a strategic risk to the
efficient functioning of the CRM in the absence of mitigation measures.
In light of these concerns the CRU has determined that the following measures should be
introduced:
•
The maximum bid volume (on a de-rated basis) of new onsite or proximate
generation and/or storage should be limited to the contracted MIC of the related new
data centre demand site in that delivery year.
•
Where the MIC is contracted to ramp, the maximum bid volume should reflect the
level of contracted MIC for that delivery year.
•
The associated new generation and/or storage can only bid for a one-year contract in
each CRM auction.
The default contract under the CRM is for 1 year, however new generation in the CRM can
apply for up to a 10-year contract. In addition, existing dispatchable generation is required to
offer all of its capacity into the CRM auction. However, for new generation linked to data
centre demand as part of this policy the above measures may need to apply. The CRU

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


54
considers that the first determination above will mitigate against the risk of surplus
generation displacing existing capacity, despite future demand growth in subsequent years.
Meanwhile, the CRU considers that limiting the contract length to one-year reduces the risk
of proximate generation securing a capacity market contract for an extended period of time
in a situation where the forecast LEU demand does not materialise or exits earlier than
planned. In cases where the generation being developed is in excess of that required to
meet the requirements in this decision, this excess generation can bid into the CRM. In such
instances, this generation is no longer eligible to contribute towards the generation
requirement for data centre capacity in future delivery years as this will already be accounted
for in the determining the CRM requirement.
The CRU notes that the implementation of these requirements may necessitate changes to
the Regulatory Authorities’ Exceptional Application process in the CRM, to auction
parameters and/or Capacity Market Code (CMC) modifications.  The CRU notes the above
requirements would likely be enforced through the contractual arrangements of the data
centre demand connection. The CRU notes that the existing CRM facilitates the signing of
new contracts up to 2028 and that new State Aid approval for a capacity mechanism will be
sought to cover the period thereafter.
3.4.5. Requirement to meet demand sites MIC
Data centres are required to provide onsite or proximate generation and/or storage with an
MEC at a level equal to or greater than their MIC (subject to derating requirements) and
acknowledging its renewable contribution (see Section 3.5 Renewable Electricity
Requirements). Some respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 expressed concerns
about the requirement for data centres to provide onsite or proximate generation matching
their MIC. These respondents suggested that this requirement is overly onerous,
economically unviable, and introduces significant financial and logistical burdens for
developers. Some respondents proposed alternative approaches they consider more flexible
and economically viable to meet energy requirements without mandating strict MIC
matching. The CRU favours an approach whereby a new data centre will be required to
provide 100% operational capacity to a level that at least covers their sites MIC (on de-rated
basis). This is to ensure that the energy requirements of the new demand site can be
accommodated by the related generation and/or storage provided. In the absence of these
provisions the connection of this demand could impact negatively on the continuity, security,
and quality of supply of electricity for the system.

text:
An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


55
3.4.6. New generation and/or storage
The CRU has determined that data centres will be required to provide onsite or proximate
generation and/or storage at a level equal to or greater than their MIC (subject to derating
requirements), with this generation being separately metered and required to participate in
the wholesale electricity market. Some respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504
requested that the policy explicitly state whether new generation is required and how it will
be defined, including its eligibility for capacity auctions and contracts. A number of
respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 emphasised the need for explicit definitions
and clarity regarding what constitutes 'new generation'. This new onsite or proximate
generation and/or storage must be new/in addition to existing generation and/or storage
operational on the system and cannot already be committed and/or accounted for through
existing market structures or mechanisms. Otherwise, these assets would not help
contribute to the additional operational electricity needs associated with a new data centre
demand connection application. For example, generation already operational in the market,
or contracted as part of the CRM, and captured within existing adequacy assessments would
not be eligible to qualify as new generation for the purposes of this policy. Use of generation
for the purposes of this policy already operational in the market, previously contracted or
committed, would likely impact on maintaining the continuity, security, and quality of supply
of electricity for the new demand itself and the wider system and as such is not permitted to
count towards this requirement.
3.4.7. De-rating of generation and/or storage
The CRU has determined that the required generation and/or storage will be de-rated by a
certain de-rating factor16 depending on its technology type and size to account for
unavailability. Many respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 expressed concerns
about the application of de-rating factors to generation and storage. Respondents argued
that de-rating factors can change over time, creating uncertainty for planning and
investment. Many respondents stated that current de-rating levels for storage are too low,
making it economically unviable. It was argued that overly stringent de-rating requirements
could deter investment in renewable and storage technologies, potentially undermining the
goals of decarbonisation and energy security.

text:
An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


56
The CRU favours an approach whereby the required generation and/or storage will be de-
rated by a certain factor depending on its technology type and size to account for its
operational characteristics e.g. whether it is energy limited, for maintenance outage
requirements, etc. The de-rating factor depends on the technology type and size and
accounts for the availability of the asset to the market. This de-rating step is to ensure that
the energy requirements of the new demand site can be reliably accommodated by the
related generation and/or storage provided on the network. In the absence of these
provisions the connection of this demand could impact negatively on the continuity, security,
and quality of supply of electricity for the system. The de-rating of storage reflects its actual
energy limited characteristics. Not reflecting these characteristics in the requirements would
impact on the effectiveness of the approach. In the scenario where generation/storage
assets were accepted without sufficient de-rating to reflect their limitations, the existing
system would be required to meet this shortfall potentially putting the security of supply of
the system at risk.
As described in Proposed Decision CRU202504 the de-rating to be applied for the purposes
of connection requirements will be informed by the de-rating curves that are published in
most recent CRM T-4 capacity auction information packs as part of the CRM auctions in the
wholesale electricity market (SEM). The CRU acknowledges that the de-rating curves
published in the CRM T-4 capacity auction information packs are updated for each auction.
In order to account for the uncertainty created by this information changing from auction to
auction, the CRU considers it appropriate that the most recent information available is used
when planning and developing projects. The de-rating information to be used to inform the
sizing of onsite or proximate generation in relation to the sites MIC will be the most recent
available at the time of the application for planning permission for the dispatchable
generation and/or storage assets.
In relation to the renewable electricity requirement as described in Section 3.5, the CRU is of
the view that the minimum of 80% of annual demand being met by renewable electricity
generated in the Republic of Ireland should be taken into account when determining the
requirement for dispatchable onsite or proximate generation in the SEM. The CRU
recognises the security of supply benefits of renewable electricity generated in the Republic
of Ireland supporting the electricity system. This associated renewable generation capacity
can be reflected on a de-rated basis against the dispatchable generation requirement.

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


57
3.4.8. Futureproof technology & storage
A number of respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 supported the future proofing of
on-site generation to ensure fuel sources can be decarbonised over time. The CRU would
encourage that any technologies used for onsite or proximate generation should be
sufficiently futureproofed where possible in terms of facilitating low/zero emissions going
forward e.g. if using gas generation, where possible and appropriate, the equipment should
be compatible with being run on lower or zero-carbon fuels. In relation to storage, the
ongoing Future Power Markets workstream by EirGrid, SONI and SEMO includes a
Scheduling and Dispatch Programme (SDP). This programme includes facilitating the
participation of energy storage such as batteries in the TSOs’ scheduling and dispatch
system.
3.4.9. Timing of demand and generation asset delivery
In Proposed Decision CRU202504 the CRU noted that there may be timing challenges in
relation to the delivery of onsite or proximate generation versus the LEU demand
connection. In Proposed Decision CRU202504 the CRU proposed to link the ramping up of a
new LEU’s demand connection towards full MIC to achieving delivery of onsite or proximate
generation and its participation in the wholesale markets. It was described that the de-rated
capacity of the onsite or proximate generation must build up in a stepwise manner in line
with demand, ensuring that the de-rated generation capacity matches the sites’ MIC at a
minimum for the duration of the connection.
Some respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 raised concerns about the practicality
of ramping requirements. Some respondents described ramping requirements as adding
complexity, time, and cost to data centre developments. Some respondents emphasised the
importance of clear definitions for ramping requirements, with clarity needed to ensure
alignment with market and regulatory frameworks. The CRU acknowledges that the timing of
the delivery of onsite or proximate dispatchable generation and/or storage capacity versus
the connection of the LEU demand will need to be managed appropriately by connection
applicants. The CRU has determined that a new data centre demand connection cannot be
operational or ramp up to its full MIC without achieving delivery of associated onsite or
proximate generation and its participation in the wholesale markets. The de-rated capacity of
the onsite or proximate generation and/or storage must at a minimum meet the ramped or
enduring MIC of the sites’ MIC for the duration of the connection and be operational. This is
to ensure that the generation and/or storage capacity is available on the system to reflect the
increased energy requirement on the system associated with the demand site, otherwise the

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


58
connection of this demand could impact negatively on the continuity, security, and quality of
supply of electricity for the system. However, the capacity of the onsite or proximate
generation and/or storage can exceed the demand site’s ramped or enduring MIC.
3.4.10. Reliability and performance of generation assets
In relation to the performance and availability of the onsite or proximate generation and/or
storage, a number of respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 provided feedback
about the reliability of generation assets, including the need for clear performance criteria,
maintenance standards, and the ability to meet demand during outages. Some respondents
emphasised how reliability is critical for ensuring uninterrupted operations and meeting
system requirements. Some respondents noted that there is a natural incentive on large
energy users to maintain their systems to ensure consistent performance and availability of
their related generation. It was suggested that de-rating factors for generation already
account for the performance and availability of generation, so stricter requirements are not
justified. It was suggested that this generation should have the same SEM rules applied to
its participation as that of other generators in the market, including performance and
availability requirements.
In the CRU’s view, the generation and/or storage associated with the data centre demand
connections greater than or equal to 10MVA should have to meet some minimum
performance and availability requirements. The de-rated capacity of the onsite or proximate
generation and/or storage must at a minimum meet the site’s MIC for the duration of the data
centre demand connection and be operational. This capacity should be made available to
the system on an operational basis in order to reflect the additional demand capacity of the
data centre and support the continuity, security, and quality of supply of electricity for the
wider system. This onsite or proximate generation and/or storage will need to be able to run
on an operational basis e.g. should not be bound by limited run hours outside of agreed
levels of routine necessary maintenance. As described in Section 3.9.3 Connection process
and assessment the CRU requires the electrical SOs to each publish an engagement and
connection process for data centre connection applicants by 31 March 2026. As part of this
process the SOs will outline minimum expected performance and availability requirements
for onsite or proximate generation and/or storage. In relation to the performance and
availability of the onsite or proximate generation and/or storage, it is envisaged that reliability
of service will be a contractual requirement for the data centre demand connection. If the
delivery, performance and availability of the onsite or proximate generation falls below this
minimum expected reliability, the SOs will have the ability to reduce the MIC of the related

arrangements.
3.4.11. Single generator for multiple data centres
In feedback to Proposed Decision CRU202504 it was queried if a single large proximate
generator can meet the requirements of a number of smaller data centres. It was queried if it
is permissible that a generator unit could assign a portion of its capacity (de-rated) to a data
centre or to multiple data centres. An example was suggested of a single 300 MW generator
allocating 100 MW to each of 3 different data centres. Insofar as the (likely proximate)
generation and/or storage is able to comply with the requirements as set out, then this
approach could be deemed acceptable. However, the CRU notes that in certain
circumstances, there may be local system reasons why the relevant SO would not be able to
accommodate generation in a ‘shared configuration’ as a solution. This assessment would
be done on a case-by-case basis by the relevant SO.
3.4.12. Mandatory Demand Curtailment
In Proposed Decision CRU202504 the CRU described how in a System Emergency State,
the SOs may instruct relevant LEUs who are subject to mandatory demand curtailment
(MDC) provisions to reduce and/or remove their demand in full from the system. It was
described how these measures can be called upon during a System Emergency State17.
Demand customers subject to MDC will be prioritised for disconnection over the
disconnection of other demand customers where practicable, but only in situations where
notice of at least 60 minutes can be provided to the relevant LEU site. LEU sites subject to
MDC provisions that receive an MDC instruction and who have not complied with that
request within the applicable timeframe may be prioritised for disconnection (without
additional notice) in advance of implementation of emergency load shedding or planned rota
load shedding. In Proposed Decision CRU202504 the CRU proposed that in light of their
contribution to the system, any data centres providing onsite or proximate dispatchable
generation as described in this section would not be required to meet MDC provisions. One
respondent to Proposed Decision CRU202504 favoured maintaining MDC on these demand
sites, describing its removal as a risk. Another respondent sought clarity in event of material
outages of associated generation. One respondent who favoured MDC not being required
linked this to the associated data centre generation meeting the SOs requirements and

60
participating in the wholesale market. This respondent suggested that failure to comply (3
strikes rule) could lead to the re-introduction of MDC measures or a reduction in MIC.
In the CRU’s view, the requirement for data centre connections to bring generation capacity
which matches the sites’ MIC means that these sites will contribute to the security of the
system. In light of this contribution to the system, the CRU has determined that any data
centres that are compliant in providing generation as described in this section will not be
required to meet MDC provisions. As noted in Proposed Decision CRU202504 all demand is
subject to potential load shedding requirements in emergency conditions as described in
CRU202346 Electricity Crises: A Risk Preparedness Plan for Ireland and data centres may
choose to sign up to MDC where appropriate to assist in managing any potential disruptions
to supply.

Decision
The Commission has made a decision that data centres with an MIC equal to or above 10
MVA connecting to the electricity network will be required to provide dispatchable onsite or
proximate generation and/or storage capacity to a level that at least covers their MIC
(subject to derating requirements), with this generation being separately connected and
metered, and required to participate in the wholesale electricity market.
The Commission has made a decision that the associated renewable generation contribution
(up to 80% annual demand) should be acknowledged and can be reflected on a de-rated
basis against the dispatchable generation requirement (see Section 3.5 Renewable
Electricity Requirement).
The Commission has made a decision that any data centres equal to or above 10 MVA and
compliant in providing onsite or proximate dispatchable generation as required under this
decision will not be required to meet MDC provisions.
The Commission has made a decision that new data centres with an MIC equal to or above
10 MVA cannot be operational or ramp up their demand without achieving delivery of
associated onsite or proximate generation. The de-rated capacity of the onsite or proximate
generation and/or storage must at a minimum meet the ramped or enduring MIC of the site
for the duration of the connection and be operational.

61
3.5. Renewable Electricity Requirement
The CRU is cognisant that Ireland has set a legally binding target of a reduction in emissions
of 51% by 2030 (compared to 2018 levels) and the Government has set sectoral emissions
targets for Ireland, as required under section 6C of the Climate Action and Low Carbon
Development Act 2015 (Climate Action Act). In addition, Ireland’s Climate Action Plan
includes a target to have up to 80% of electricity generated from renewable sources by
2030.
Section 3.1 “Emissions remit” of this document sets out the CRU’s interpretation of its
responsibilities under the Climate Action Act, namely that the Climate Action Act does not
confer any additional functions on the CRU but places it under an obligation to perform its
current functions in a manner consistent with the objectives and policies in section 15(1)(a)–
(e) insofar as practicable. The CRU does not consider, therefore, that the Climate Action Act
confers a statutory function on the CRU to set a connection policy other than in line with the
CRU’s other existing statutory functions. The CRU has no existing statutory function in the
1999 Act or otherwise that allows it to set express requirements for emissions reduction
and/or offsetting measures. In contrast, under section 9(1)(s) of the 1999 Act, the CRU has
the statutory function of ensuring that grid connection policy takes account of renewable
energy policy.
3.5.1. Earlier consultations
In Call for Evidence CRU202357 and Consultation CRU2024001 the CRU outlined a number
of potential different approaches to decarbonise LEU demand. This included through on-site
electricity generation such as solar and/or wind. If on-site dispatchable generation was to be
used, it was described how the fuel for this could be sourced exclusively from renewable
sources (e.g. sufficient certified renewable gas feeding into the Irish system). It was
suggested that if on-site battery storage was being used, the fuel for this could be sourced
exclusively from renewable sources, e.g. by securing sufficient renewable electricity feeding
into the Irish system. For electricity consumption it was described how Corporate Power
Purchase Agreements (CPPAs) could support additionality of indigenous renewable
generation outside of support schemes, with renewable electricity feeding into the Irish
system and certified renewable gas feeding into Irish gas network. These provisions were to
ensure that the associated renewable electricity and /or gas would contribute to Ireland’s
emissions targets and security of supply.
In feedback to these papers, some respondents favoured the use of CPPAs for additionality
of renewable generation outside of Government support schemes for decarbonising

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


62
electricity consumption. Challenges such as having adequate space for sufficient onsite
renewables were raised, and it was suggested that the use of CPPAs would be essential to
some developers, with on-site generation and CPPAs seen as complementary. CPPAs were
described as the most effective instrument to facilitate new renewables, and to support the
core investment required to make these projects financeable. It was suggested that CPPAs
may support more marginal storage and conversion projects such as pumped hydro that
may otherwise have difficulty in finding a route to market.
Some respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 suggested mandating renewable
energy use, promoting CPPAs, and ensuring renewable energy additionality to meet
Ireland's climate targets. CPPAs were highlighted by respondents as a significant
mechanism for data centres to meet renewable energy goals, with some respondents
highlighting existing commitments to meet at least 30-50% of annual site electricity demand
through CPPAs. Some respondents proposed more ambitious goals for CPPAs, including
real-time net-zero energy matching and hourly emissions reporting. It was suggested a glide
path could be developed toward achieving 24/7 renewable energy matching.

3.5.2. Level of renewable electricity required
In Call for Evidence CRU202357 and Consultation CRU2024001 the CRU considered what
target level LEUs carbon emissions should be measured to. For instance, should the end
target/goal for new LEUs be close to real time zero emissions or measured over a set time
period e.g. on an annual basis. Some respondents raised concerns that achieving closer to
real time net zero emissions from LEUs at the time of connection was not practical in the
short term, with some suggesting it would be unworkable. As described in CRU2024001 the
CRU sees merit in implementing a transition period in order to facilitate the development and
maturation of different options/approaches in how LEUs can meet the real time net zero
emissions challenge. A benefit to the use of a glide path/transition period is that it can
facilitate the path to an end target allowing progress on an incremental basis, for example
allowing for an appropriate progression towards requiring closer to real time renewable
energy requirements for new LEU connection applications in the future.
The CRU sees merit in requiring new data centre connections to meet a certain percentage
of their demand with renewable electricity generated in the Republic of Ireland such as
through CPPAs or direct development of renewable generation assets in order to contribute
towards Ireland’s renewable energy targets. This renewable electricity contribution could be
measured on an annual basis. The Climate Action Plan includes measures to increase the

source_reference.locator: page 63, section 3.5.2. Level of renewable electricity required

text:
An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


63
proportion of renewable electricity to up to 80% by 2030. In order to ensure progress
towards reaching these national targets, the CRU considers it to be appropriate to require
new data centres captured under this policy to provide or procure additional renewable
electricity generated in the Republic of Ireland (e.g. CPPAs with wind, solar etc) physically
feeding into the Irish electricity network which meet at least 80% of the data centres demand
on an annual basis. This requirement reflects the current renewable electricity target and
may be reviewed if the target is revised. In meeting this renewable electricity requirement,
the actual output of the renewable generation facility should be considered. This means that
the location and network infrastructure in the locality of the renewable project are important
factors in so far as they may have an effect on the actual output of a project. Renewable
generation to meet this requirement must be generated in the Republic of Ireland and be
new/in addition to renewable generation which is or has been operational on the system.
Renewable generation which has previously been or is currently contracted through existing
support mechanisms (e.g. REFIT, RESS, ORESS) cannot be used to meet this requirement.
Provision or procurement of the minimum level of renewable electricity generation will be a
contractual requirement, as set out in more detail in sub-section 3.5.7. This provision is
designed to reduce the risk of this policy inadvertently undermining the state led renewable
energy support schemes and achievement of the Government’s renewable energy targets.
Where full repowering of a renewable electricity project takes place, i.e. the project
undergoes decommissioning and replacement of equipment, this can be considered to be
eligible for a CPPA to meet the requirements of this policy.
3.5.3. Reflecting renewable electricity contribution
The CRU favours an approach which acknowledges a new data centres’ contribution of
additional renewable energy outside of state support schemes. The CRU recognises the
security of supply benefits of renewable electricity generated in the Republic of Ireland
supporting the electricity system.  The CRU is of the view that up to the 80% annual
renewable electricity match should be taken into account when determining the requirements
for autoproduction or dispatchable onsite or proximate generation in the SEM (e.g. meeting
the MIC on de-rated basis). In cases where a data centre chooses to develop or contract
annual renewable electricity generated in the Republic of Ireland in excess of 80% of their
annual demand, only renewable generation contracted to deliver up to the 80% of annual
demand will be considered (on de-rated basis) for contributing towards dispatchable
generation requirement. This associated renewable generation would be reflected on a de-
rated basis against the dispatchable generation requirement.

generation could be facilitated via CPPA or directly developed renewable assets. This will
help ensure additionality of renewables e.g. renewable energy projects not facilitated

•
Ability of applicant to meet at least 80% of their annual demand through provision or

(e.g. through CPPAs with wind, solar etc, or through direct development of renewable

In the above criterion, the CRU has specified renewable electricity generated in the Republic
of Ireland, i.e. renewable electricity feeding into the Irish system. This provision is to ensure
the associated renewable electricity contributes to Ireland’s renewable electricity targets and
security of supply.

3.5.6. Timing of delivery of renewable electricity requirements (development
timeframe)
One challenge that was highlighted through feedback was the challenge in having
renewable generation projects delivered at the same time or in advance of the energisation
of the data centre demand. Challenges were highlighted in terms of the volume of renewable
projects available in the pipeline, and time required to develop these. The option of requiring
renewable generation to be in place at the time of connection and energisation of the data
centre may present a risk to the pipeline of projects being delivered through RESS rather
than new projects being developed to meet the data centre demand. One possible option
would be to provide some flexibility in the timing of delivery of the renewable generation,
however any delay in this would impact on the ability of data centres to contribute towards
Ireland’s renewable electricity targets immediately upon connection and energisation of a
data centre. The CRU acknowledges the challenges associated with the delivery timeframe
for renewable energy projects and sees merit in allowing a transition period for new data
centre connections to build up to meet at least 80% of their annual demand with renewable
electricity generated in the Republic of Ireland. In order to reflect these timing challenges,
the CRU considers that new data centres should have a 6-year glide path from the date of a
data centre demand site’s energisation to build up to meet at least 80% of demand with

renewable electricity generated in the Republic of Ireland on an annual basis. The 6-year
transition period facilitates the gradual build-up of renewable electricity either through direct
development of renewable generation or contracting through a CPPA to meet the
requirement of at least 80% of the data centres annual demand.
The CRU considers that a 6-year transition period provides an appropriate balance between
accounting for the timeline associated with renewable energy project development in Ireland,
while also ensuring the renewable generation is in place in a timely manner. In the 2019
IWEA report titled “Life-cycle of an Onshore Wind Farm20” it describes the different phases of
development of a project (feasibility, planning and permitting, pre-construction, construction,
commissioning). The report shows estimated timelines ranging from approximately 5 to 10
years to complete these stages and become operational. In determining the appropriate
timeline, the CRU has given consideration to the current development timelines for
renewable energy projects, the permitting timelines required under RED III and the timelines
for delivery of projects under the Renewable Electricity Support Scheme (RESS). The CRU
is cognisant of the need for additionality of renewables and considers that this timeframe will
allow for greater additionality (i.e. delivery of new renewable electricity projects), rather than
being met solely by the existing pipeline of new renewable electricity projects. For projects
that have been unsuccessful in RESS/ORESS auctions, a CPPA with a data centre can
provide an alternative route to market. In many cases these projects will be further along the
development pipeline and may not proceed in the absence of a long-term contract such as a
CPPA. As part of their grid connection application, applicants will be required to demonstrate
a credible plan (e.g. would identify the specific renewable generation that will support the
projects and the anticipated timeline for development) in relation to how they intend to meet
at least 80% of their annual demand with renewable electricity generated in the Republic of
Ireland within a 6-year period from the date of the demand site’s energisation. Although a
transition period is being provided to reach 80% of demand with renewable electricity on an
annual basis, the CRU notes that early connection of renewable energy will deliver benefits
to the system, consumers and developers and would encourage connection of renewable
energy associated with meeting this requirement to be as expedient as possible.

3.5.7. Compliance with requirements
Provision or procurement of the minimum level of renewable electricity generation will be a
contractual requirement, set out in the contractual arrangements by the relevant System
Operator. As part of their application, the data centre developer will be required to submit a
credible plan (e.g. identifying the specific renewable generation projects and the anticipated
timeline for development) in relation to how they intend to meet at least 80% of their annual
demand with renewable electricity generated in the Republic of Ireland within a 6-year period
from the date of the demand site’s energisation. This credible plan must take into account
the expected output of the renewable generation facility. This means that the location and
network infrastructure in the locality of the renewable project are important factors in so far as
they may have an effect on the actual output of a project.  Data centres will be required to
report annually on progress towards and compliance with this requirement. Data centres will
have the time during the development of the data centre and then an additional 6-year glide
path from the date of the demand sites energisation to directly develop or contract with
sufficient renewable electricity generated in the Republic of Ireland in order to meet the
minimum 80% renewable electricity requirements. If a party to a data centre connection
agreement fails to meet the minimum 80% renewable energy generated in the Republic of
Ireland requirement following the end of the 6-year glide path, the SOs will have the ability to
reduce the MIC of the related data centre’s demand connection to the level met successfully
by 80% renewable electricity. This should be set out by the SOs within the contractual
arrangements. The CRU is also cognisant that there may be some aspects beyond the
control of the party to a data centre that could result in a delay to the delivery of the
renewable energy projects. As part of the implementation of this decision, the SOs will
develop a ruleset for how to assess this requirement, including how to address instances of
non-compliance in a fair and transparent way.
Section 3.8 Renewable Electricity Reporting Requirements provides further information on
reporting requirements that will be included in the connection conditions for new data centre
connections. The CRU may review these requirements going forward, for instance if national
renewable energy targets are updated.

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


69
Decision
The Commission has made a decision to require data centres with an MIC equal to or above
the de-minimis level to meet at least 80% of their annual demand with additional renewable
electricity generated in the Republic of Ireland.
The Commission has made a decision that new data centre should have a 6-year glide path
from the date of demand site’s energisation in order to meet the requirement of at least 80%
of demand with renewable electricity generated in the Republic of Ireland on annual basis.
The Commission has made a decision that as part of their grid connection application,
applicants will be required to demonstrate a credible plan (e.g. would identify the specific
renewable generation that will support the projects and the anticipated timeline for
development) in relation to how they intend to meet renewable electricity requirement.


3.6. Location
3.6.1. Constraints on the electrical system and location
In Proposed Decision CRU202504, Section 2 ‘Constrained regions of the electrical system
and security of supply’ sets out some of the system and capacity challenges faced on the
electricity system, and the location specific characteristics of some of these. In previous
papers such as consultation CRU2024001 the locational aspect of LEUs was discussed,
describing how the CRU sees merit in locating new LEUs close to renewable generation and
storage, and being located outside of constrained areas on the grid. In Proposed Decision
CRU202504 the CRU proposed that the SOs should take into account the location of the
requested connection (to include the demand and the associated onsite/proximate
generation) in respect of whether it is in a constrained or unconstrained region, in
considering whether a connection offer can be made, citing the impact of local and regional
system conditions on any new data centre demand connections, and vice versa. This was
consistent with aspects of the decision made in CRU/21/124 in relation to Data Centre grid
connection processing and related direction to the SOs.
3.6.2. Greater Dublin region constraints
In Proposed Decision CRU202504 it described some of the system challenges around the
Dublin region. It was described how the rapid increase in demand from data centre

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


70
customers in the general Dublin region had placed significant pressures on the local system
and generation capacity requirements. In the All-island Resource Adequacy Assessment
2025–2034 EirGrid describe how based on their annual review of data centres and new
technology loads, demand is expected to continue to rise from current levels as these
customers build out towards their contracted load. EirGrid describe how almost all this extra
load is contracted in the greater Dublin region and was contracted prior to the CRU 2021
direction which brought additional requirements on new applicants. Proposed Decision
CRU202504 described EirGrid’s Local Security of Supply multi-year plan 2023-2027 which
identifies the infrastructure delivery actions and activities that EirGrid will undertake during
the period to contribute to the resolution of security of supply issues in the greater Dublin
region. Within this document EirGrid reference the Powering Up Dublin programme21 which
is an integrated programme of works to update and transform the Dublin Area electricity
transmission network.
In Proposed Decision CRU202504 it also described how short circuit current/fault levels in
the Dublin region are a challenge, referring to an EirGrid report from October 202322. It
described how EirGrid indicated that this is a safety and system security issue and is related
to the amount of generation connected in the Dublin area and the topology of the
transmission network. EirGrid set out how Dublin has a high concentration of synchronous
generators, with the highly meshed Dublin network. In their Short Circuit Summary for
Industry23 from March 2025, EirGrid described that the main sources of short-circuit currents
are conventional generators, synchronous condensers, and induction machines. It describes
how renewable sources and inverter-based resources also produce short-circuit currents,
and generator transformers change the impedance of the network, exacerbating the issue.
EirGrid described how Dublin (and to a lesser extent Cork) is where the issue has now
manifested due to the need to run a lot of conventional generation at times to manage power
flows and other constraints arising from the rapid development experienced in this area.
3.6.3. Constraints outside the Dublin region
Proposed Decision CRU202504 referred to EirGrid’s Shaping our Electricity Future V1.1
paper, which outlined that outside of the Dublin region EirGrid has updated its assumptions

3.6.4. Feedback to Proposed Decision CRU202504 on location and constraints
Some respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 discussed the significant challenges
posed by network constraints, particularly in the Greater Dublin Area. It was described how
these constraints affect grid capacity, security of supply, and the ability to accommodate new
connections, including data centres. Some respondents identified data centres as major
contributors to electricity demand and network constraints. It was described how rapid
growth in data centres is surpassing the pace of grid infrastructure development, creating
pressures on the network. Some respondents described how the Greater Dublin Area,
including counties Dublin, Meath, and Kildare, were identified as a Tier 1 location for data
centre connectivity. One respondent highlighted that where there is a high concentration of
data centres, for example in Dublin, and as such that there is the potential for exceeding air
quality standards for NOx, especially if generators across several of the data storage
facilities operate simultaneously with each other and power plants or other licensed activities
in the area. Some responses to Proposed Decision CRU202504 highlighted the need for
flexibility in locational policies, suggesting that overly rigid constraints could hinder
innovation and development. Some respondents called for the need for principled, site-
specific assessments and avoiding overly restrictive locational policies. It was proposed that
blanket constraints could be removed. A number of respondents to Proposed Decision
CRU202504 stated the “Constrained Area Construct” is redundant in a context where LEU’s
have independent generation coupled with the capability to deliver a “real-time” flexible
connection to the System Operator. These respondents suggested that maintaining this
construct will exclude most developments, existing and planned, and amounts to an effective
retention of the current moratorium.

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


72
Some respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 described how data centres have
significantly contributed to Ireland's economy, generating billions of Euro in terms of
economic benefits, creating thousands of jobs, and supporting ICT services exports. It was
described how their development is vital for Ireland's position as a global technology hub.
Some respondents stated the location of data centres near interconnected metro areas is
critical for their success. It was suggested Ireland's foundational infrastructure offers
opportunities for digital investment, but competition with other jurisdictions must be
considered. Some respondents stated that energy policy uncertainty and grid connection
challenges are deterring Foreign Direct Investment and data centre expansion in Ireland. It
was suggested that addressing these issues is crucial to maintain Ireland's attractiveness for
investment.
3.6.5. Impact of location
As described in Proposed Decision CRU202504 the CRU recognises the challenges of
connecting in constrained areas or areas where there are short circuit issues, and where the
connection of large demands in these areas in advance of infrastructure development poses
a risk to system security standards and supply to new and existing customers. The potential
scale and speed of increase of potential new data centre demand in relation to local system
conditions, means that existing constraints may be exacerbated or new ones created in
previously unconstrained parts of the system. The CRU considers that taking account of
location in respect of whether a connection is in a constrained or unconstrained location
remains a relevant and important consideration. The CRU notes that this assessment should
not be on a wide geographical/regional basis, and instead a more localised consideration of
constraints and solutions should be carried out by the relevant SO. As outlined in Section
3.7.3, it is expected that a framework on flexible connections will be developed in due
course.
As described above the CRU considers that it is necessary and proportionate to require new
data centres above the de-minimis level (1MVA) to provide onsite or proximate generation
and/or storage or autoproducer (depending on demand size) that will participate in the
wholesale electricity market. This is to ensure the continuity, security, and quality of supply
of electricity is maintained. The CRU favours this centrally dispatched approach for this
requirement which will help facilitate the optimum solution on a whole system operational
basis where possible via existing market structures. As the CRU noted in Proposed Decision
CRU202504 a connection application seeking a certain level of demand and associated
generation could have an effect on the constraint status of an area if it were to proceed. In

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


73
some cases, the requirement to bring onsite or proximate generation may add to the
constraint, e.g. in areas where there are high short circuit levels on the existing network, the
addition of synchronous generation can exacerbate safety risks. Therefore, there may be
areas of the network where further connections may not be available in the absence of
reinforcements and upgrades. Given the uncertainty of future demand requirements, this
may require consideration as part of the network development planning process.
Based on the above considerations, the CRU has determined that the SOs should take into
account the location of the requested connection (to include the demand and the associated
onsite/proximate generation) in respect of whether it is in a constrained or unconstrained
location, in considering whether a connection offer can be made. It is within the SOs remit to
determine whether a connection can or cannot be accommodated based on their
assessment of each application. As described above the CRU notes that this assessment
should not be on a wide geographical/regional basis, and instead a more localised
consideration of constraints and the specific impact a proposed data centre (including the
necessary generation) is expected to have on the grid. This approach will help account for
the potential impact of local and regional system conditions on any new data centre demand
connections, and vice versa. The CRU considers that the SOs taking into account the
location of the requested connection as an important step to protect against risks to system
security standards. In a scenario where a connection application cannot be facilitated the
relevant SO should provide sufficient detail to the applicant on why this outcome occurred,
and reasons provided shall be based on objective and justified criteria.
3.6.6. Publication of network information
As described in Proposed Decision CRU202504 in order to provide more clarity to potential
connection applicants on the areas of the electricity network that are constrained and the
areas where the SOs are planning network reinforcements, the CRU is of the view that the
SOs will need to provide accessible information in relation to locations that are constrained
or likely to become constrained. This includes information on the network capacity currently
available across the electricity networks and that which will become available under network
development plans.

distribution network and can signal future capacity changes. Since the publication of
Proposed Decision CRU202504, ESB Networks have published an Available Capacity Map34

to make detailed information relating to network capacity on the electricity system easily
accessible to ensure greater visibility to inform appropriate locations for connection to the
network.
Some respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 supported the need for more network
information being provided, emphasising the importance of SOs providing regular,
transparent updates on network constraints. Some respondents suggested the inclusion of
detailed, color-coded maps, indicative timelines for grid reinforcements, and clarity on
constrained and unconstrained areas to aid in planning and decision-making. Some
respondents requested more granular and specific information, such as substation-level
details, to better understand constraints. Some respondents suggested this will help in
aligning demand with available capacity, reducing inefficiencies, and supporting the
development of renewable energy projects. The CRU notes the benefits of having more
regular detailed information relating to network capacity made available to potential future
connection applicants, giving greater transparency and helping to inform stakeholder
investment decisions.
The CRU requires the System Operators to make detailed information relating to network
capacity on the electricity system easily accessible so that there can be greater visibility to
the investment community in relation to appropriate locations for development.  The
publication of network information should:
1. Enhance transparency and accessibility of data
2. Clearly demonstrate the impact of the implementation of network development plans
3. Be updated frequently (quarterly, moving closer to real-time)
4. Use clear and consistent definitions throughout
5. Provide a coordinated and integrated view of distribution and transmission system
capacity.

The CRU expects that the network information provided by the SOs would include the
following:
•
Heatmaps/information illustrating current and projected capacity availability at
different nodes/substations.
o This should account for the capacity which is already contracted.
o Information on capacity that is expected to be taken up by projected growth
(e.g. electrification of transport and housing, planned new housing
development and other social needs) should be included.
o The information should also account for other limitations at substation level
such as availability of bays at substation, thermal limits, short-circuit capacity,
space constraints and other factors which may impact the ability to connect at
this location.
o TSO and DSO information should be integrated to take into account upstream
capacity, e.g. available transmission capacity upstream from a Bulk Supply
Point.
•
Forward looking heatmaps/information illustrating capacity which is due to become
available based on network development plans accounting for the capacity which will
be taken up by projected growth, and the associated timelines for additional capacity
and future network delivery.
•
Greater visibility of network development plans.
As described in Proposed Decision CRU202504 the granularity of information should be
sufficient to help inform potential new connection applicants (demand and generation) in
terms of viable areas for connection. This information should be provided on a sufficiently
regular basis to ensure it is up to date to inform potential connection applicants, for instance
on a quarterly basis, and moving closer to real time. As noted in Proposed Decision
CRU202504 given the interaction between capacity availability on the distribution and
transmission systems, there is a need for interaction between ESB Networks and EirGrid in
relation to developing and publishing the required information. This is also aligned with the
requirements under Regulation 2024/1747 which states ‘Distribution system operators and
transmission system operators shall cooperate with each other in publishing, in a consistent
manner, consistent information on the capacity available for new connections in their
respective areas of operation that provides sufficient granular visibility to developers of new
energy projects and other potential network users’.

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


77
The CRU requests proposals from the System Operators outlining a plan for delivery of the
requirements set out above and under Directive (EU) 2024/1711 (Article 2) & Regulations
(EU) 2024/1747, the integration of information provision for the transmission and
distributions systems, what measures are currently in place and what network information
can be made available in the near term.
The CRU requests the two SOs to provide initial proposals in relation to these requirements,
including plans to ensure consistency and integration between information provision relating
to the transmission and distribution systems, by31 March 2026. The CRU envisages that this
work will likely require ongoing engagement between the CRU and SOs in due course in
order to achieve the above requirements and benefits.

Decision
The Commission has made a decision that the SOs should take into account the location of
the requested data centre connection application and associated generation in respect of if it
is in a constrained or unconstrained location on the electricity network. It is within the SOs
remit to determine whether a connection can or cannot be accommodated based on their
assessment of each application.
The Commission requires the SOs to publish regular up to date locational information
(existing and outlook) in relation to the availability of capacity on the electricity network and
network constraint. The SOs are to provide to the CRU, initial proposals in relation to these
requirements by 31 March 2026.


3.7. Demand flexibility & flexible connections
In the Call for Evidence (CRU202357), Consultation (CRU2024001) and Proposed Decision
(CRU202504) papers the use of demand flexibility in the context of this review of LEU
connection policy was explored. It was described how effective demand flexibility is a key
element in supporting the electricity system and supporting a higher proportion of renewable
energy on the system. Leveraging demand flexibility could help support the reliability and
operation of the electricity network while enabling decarbonisation by making better use of
renewable energy sources. It was described in Proposed Decision CRU202504 how as part
