78
of the Climate Action Plan (CAP24)36, a key measure to manage electricity demand flexibility
and growth is that the CRU will deliver an Electricity Demand Side Strategy and
Implementation Plan (action number EL/23/24), with the aim of 20 to 30% of electricity
demand to be flexible by 2030 (15-20% flexibility by 2025). In fulfilment of this action, the
CRU published the National Energy Demand Strategy37 (or NEDS) in July 2024.
It was described in the previous papers how demand flexibility can mean a site increasing or
decreasing demand from the grid in response to certain signals/information. This could be
facilitated by load-shifting, i.e. an LEU moving tasks/workloads to different times, or it could
mean using onsite storage or back up generation to supply onsite load or feed into the grid.
Proposed Decision CRU202504 cited how the NEDS decision paper determined that
demand flexibility will be defined as the percentage of average daily demand (MWh) that can
be flexed up or down.
Some respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 favoured enabling some form of
demand response or flexibility as part of the connection requirements. However, many
respondents saw this as a substitute for some or all of the requirement to provide proximate
or on-site generation and/or storage which matches the demand sites MIC on de-rated
basis. Some respondents described requiring both flexibility and proximate and/or onsite
generation as onerous, as this could require data centres to provide power for export to the
grid and for their own consumption simultaneously. Some respondents described flexibility
as a less carbon intensive and more efficient method of addressing capacity and constraint
issues on the system. Some described it as a temporary measure only required until system
adequacy issues are addressed. Some respondents highlighted the need for smarter
dispatch and forecasting systems for demand response and flexibility.
3.7.1. Provision for demand flexibility in direction
In Proposed Decision CRU202504 the CRU stated that, in light of the requirement for data
centre connections to bring onsite or proximate dispatchable generation capacity which, at a
minimum, matches the sites’ MIC, the CRU does not propose mandating an additional
requirement that connection applications falling under this policy must also provide a
demand flexibility contribution to the system. In Proposed Decision CRU202504 it described
how the CRU sees merit in the System Operators having the ability to require demand

flexibility from data centres on the local system as deemed necessary on a case-by-case

The CRU considers that requirements under this decision for data centres to provide onsite

the generation when required. However, the CRU notes that there may be significant
opportunities for data centres to participate in demand flexibility measures such as those
outlined below, which may provide additional revenue streams while supporting system
needs. A number of these initiatives are in early stages of development and opportunities
may emerge as they are rolled out in future.
3.7.2. Dispatchable demand flexibility schemes
In Proposed Decision CRU202504 it described how it is envisaged that a new formalised
scheme(s) and related product(s) will be implemented by the SOs to facilitate dispatchable
demand flexibility from LEUs on a regular operational basis. It is envisaged that these

•
Beat the Peak: In 2022 ESB Networks introduced Beat the Peak, as part of the
National Network, Local Connections Programme. Beat the Peak is a collection of

times that put strain on the network, towards times of lower carbon supply.

3.7.3. Flexible connections
The Electricity Market Design Directive (EU) 2024/171140 sets out a number of different
provisions including the requirement for Member States to develop a framework for the TSO
and DSO to offer the possibility of establishing flexible connections in areas where there is
limited or no network capacity availability for new connections. The Department of  Climate,
Energy and the Environment (DCEE) published a consultation41 on 15 October 2024 to seek
views in assisting the transposition of this directive into Irish law, including whether the CRU
as the regulatory authority, or another competent authority, shall develop this framework and
have authority over this provision. Following this consultation process, it is envisaged that
the New Electricity Market Design Directive will be transposed into Irish law and that CRU
will be designated as the competent authority. It is expected that following the confirmation
of these developments in a corresponding decision by the Department of Climate, Energy
and the Environment the CRU will develop a framework on flexible connections in due
course.
Several respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 suggested that data centres could be
given flexible connections or other similar arrangements whereby the demand site could
“come off” the network during times of constraint or system tightness. At present there are a
limited number of examples of flexible demand connections in Ireland, these include:
•
Flexible Demand Operating Protocol: The Flexible Demand Operating Protocol was
introduced as a requirement for a number of connecting data centres. In this
approach EirGrid retains the right to instruct the data centre to lower its power
consumption after exhausting other hierarchical actions, such as dispatching
available relevant generation and DSUs. This protocol would be activated to avoid
entering an alert state if there is a shortage of generation, or to help alleviate a local
constraint. It would not be classified as a TSO action in wholesale markets, as it does
not involve a registered market unit, nor would it fall under the current Grid Code
definition of "Demand Control".
•
ESB Networks Timed Connections Pilot: A Timed Connections pilot is being
progressed as part of ESB Networks’ innovation programme and seeks to increase
existing network utilisation and allow faster connection timelines for customers. ESB

Networks have proposed to offer certain eligible customers the opportunity to have
additional import capacity, on a time restricted basis, when the network is traditionally
less congested e.g. night-time. These timed connections may allow for increased
capacity at specific times of the day, but in future could extend to specific days of the
week or times of the year.
•
ESB Networks Flexible Demand Connections Initiative: ESB Networks is developing
a process for Flexible Demand Connections, allowing for an increase in Maximum
Import Capacity (MIC) at a connection, subject to specific conditions. Under this
initiative, which is currently very limited in scope, participants agree to lower their
peak demand when required by ESB Networks in exchange for a higher flexible MIC
in constrained areas, allowing for faster connection times. During high-demand
periods with grid constraints, ESB Networks can instruct the customer to reduce
consumption up to the agreed amount in line with the flexible proportion of the MIC.
This is a temporary arrangement pending grid reinforcements. Once the necessary
network upgrades are in places the connection will be deemed firm. As part of the
conditions when accepting a flexible connection, a customer must comply with
instructions to reduce consumption, failure to do so could result in disconnection.
It should be noted that these initiatives are still at an early stage and are limited in scale.
Learnings from these arrangements will help to inform the future framework for flexible
connections, taking into account aspects such as control, measurement, reliability and
scalability.

3.8. Reporting Requirements
3.8.1. Proposed decision
In Proposed Decision CRU202504 it described how the CRU proposed to require regular
reporting on renewable energy use and emissions by data centres to system operators, a
summary of which would be published by the system operators.
In Proposed Decision CRU202504 the CRU noted that there are a number of initiatives
underway relating to reporting requirements for data centres and LEUs.

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


83
The Energy Efficiency Directive42 includes requirements to collect and publish data on the
energy performance, water footprint, and demand side flexibility of data centres, to
contribute towards increasing efficiency and promote decarbonisation of the grid. The
Energy Efficiency Directive is supplemented by Regulation 2024/1364 on the first phase of
the establishment of a common Union rating scheme for data centres. This Regulation sets
out the information and key performance indicators (KPIs) to be communicated to the
European database by the operators of data centres with an installed information technology
power demand of at least 500 kW and are necessary for the establishment of a common
Union scheme for rating the sustainability of data centres in the EU, as well as a common
measurement and calculation methodology. It also defines the first data centre sustainability
indicators that will be calculated based on the information and key performance indicators
communicated to the European database on data centres. The focus on KPIs such as
energy consumption, renewable energy use, waste heat reuse, and water input ensures that
data centres are continuously monitored for environmental performance.
The Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive43 (Directive (EU) 2022/2464) requires
companies to disclose how sustainability risks impact them and how their operations impact
society and the environment. This directive supports the EU’s Green Deal objectives by
ensuring that corporate practices are aligned with resource efficiency and the transition to
climate neutrality by 2050.
In Proposed Decision CRU202504 the CRU noted that Action EL/24/22 in the 2024 Climate
Action Plan sets out that SEAI /CRU /EirGrid /ESBN are to deliver the ‘Implementation of
enhanced emissions reporting framework for electricity emissions for large energy users and
the system operators dispatch actions’. As part of this action, SEAI published the ‘LEU
electricity emissions reporting framework – Recommendations for design and
implementation’44. This report sets out high-level recommendations for how such a
framework could be structured.

Many respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 emphasised the importance of
renewable energy procurement and emissions reporting. Many respondents emphasised the

3.8.3. Reporting requirements
As described Section “3.5 Renewable Electricity Requirement” the CRU has made a
decision to require data centres to match at least 80% of their annual demand with additional
renewable electricity generated in the Republic of Ireland, e.g. through direct development of
renewable assets or through CPPAs. The CRU notes that data centres will be required to
report to the SOs on their compliance with this requirement, which will be covered under the
data centre’s contractual arrangements.
The CRU notes that Article 12 of the Energy Efficiency Directive requires data centres
(defined by the directive as falling into three categories: enterprise, colocation and co-
hosting) to report publicly on their energy performance annually. The key performance
indicators to be set out are specified in Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364
of 14 March 2024 and include measures relating to consumption of renewables, inter alia,
•
Total renewable energy consumption
•

•
Total renewable energy consumption from Power Purchasing Agreements
•
Total renewable energy consumption from on-site renewables
Following engagement with DCEE, the CRU expects that the transposition of the Energy
Efficiency Directive will require individual data centres to report publicly on the measures
referred to above. This is in line with the proposals within the CRU’s Proposed Decision
CRU202504. Taking into account this development and the feedback to the proposed
decision in relation to existing mechanisms to fulfil the reporting requirement, the CRU

The CRU notes that the reporting requirement covered by the EED may include renewables
contracted under CPPAs in Ireland and in other countries, some of which may be covered by
imported GoOs. Given that the renewable electricity requirement set out in Section 3.5
Renewable Electricity Requirement is intended to assist in the delivery of the national 80%
renewables target as set out in the Climate Action Plan and contribute to security of supply,
the data centres will be required to indicate to the SOs specifically the renewables
connected or contracted on the Republic of Ireland system by the LEUs.
The CRU also acknowledges that work is ongoing in relation to the LEU electricity emissions
reporting framework. As capability is developed in this area it is envisaged that data centres
which fall under the framework will be required to report their emissions on an hourly

Decision
The Commission has made a decision that data centres will be required to report to the SOs

3.9. Connection Process, Assessment and Enforcement
3.9.1. Proposed decision
In Proposed Decision CRU202504 it described how it is envisaged that the SOs will assess
applications at the connection application stage to assess whether the proposed measures
meet the requirements outlined. Where the SO is not satisfied by reference to the
assessment criteria that a connection offer can be made to an applicant consistent with the
needs of the electricity system, the application will not be processed by the SO, accordingly,
the application will terminate.

3.9.2. Proposed Decision CRU202504 feedback
Some respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 raised challenges such as practical
issues in connection agreements and engagement levels with system operators during the
connection process. Some respondents emphasised the importance of stakeholder
engagement through workshops, transparent review processes, and regular updates on
policy and decision-making. It was suggested these measures could streamline connection

and EirGrid prior to an application for planning permission being submitted will also be

Some respondents called for clear and published criteria for connection decisions, along with
a transparent review and appeals process to ensure accountability and fairness in the
termination of applications. Some respondents emphasised the need for clear and updated

reviewing and updating the Data Centre Connection Offer Process and Policy, outlining
criteria for application acceptance, and ensuring transparency in decision-making. In
feedback to Proposed Decision CRU202504 the unilateral termination of connection
applications was raised as a significant concern, marking a divergence from established
engagements and raising questions about fairness and transparency. One respondent
raised issue with the application of any new direction to existing applications being
processed. This respondent highlighted the wording change from 'all new connection
applications contracts' to 'all new connection contracts'. This respondent stated the CRU
should not subject current applications being processed or terminations being appealed or

3.9.3. Connection process and assessment
The CRU notes respondents’ comments seeking clear assessment criteria and connection
processes. The CRU notes that this policy decision will apply to all new connection
applications for new or additional capacity captured under the scope of the decision.
Direction CRU/21/124 will be superseded by the new direction to the SOs as set out in
Section 6.2.  As part of this new direction, the CRU is requiring the SOs to publish a clear
and transparent engagement and connection application process for data centres reflecting
the decisions stated in this paper. The CRU expects that the process will set out the
following:
Stages of the process: The relevant stages of the connection process and the
associated indicative timelines, including proposals for early engagement for data centre
applicants.
Application Requirements: The SOs should set out the requirements for a complete
project application including a template application form, requirements for supporting
documentation (including any relevant planning permission requirements, proof of
generation, etc.), and any applicable fees. These requirements should be based on the
assessment criteria outlined in this decision, along with other information that the SOs
deem relevant.
Offer process: SOs to provide clarity on the type of information and requirements that
would be included in a connection offer.
The SOs are subject to EU obligations to improve transparency around grid connection
capacity under Article 50(4a) of Regulation (EU) 2019/943, as amended by Regulation (EU)
2024/1711, and separately, under Directive (EU) 2024/1771, which amends Directive (EU)
2019/944. Both provisions aim to support efficient grid access and planning. While this
information is not a guarantee of capacity, any prospective applicant should refer to any
available network information prior to contact with the SOs’ to ensure their proposal has
potential to be feasible. As set out in Section 3.6.6 Publication of Network Information, the
CRU requires the System Operators to make detailed information relating to network
capacity on the electricity system easily accessible so that there can be greater visibility to
the investment community in relation to appropriate locations for development.

The CRU acknowledges that new project applicants/developers may require early
engagement with the relevant SO in order to inform a number of different project design
elements. These early engagements could provide information relating to constrained
locations and help inform the proximate generation specification and siting, and whether the
proposed approach would be deemed acceptable to the relevant SO. The CRU recognises
that SO resources should be targeted towards more advanced projects, and that a certain
level of project maturity may need to be demonstrated to enter into the pre-engagement
process. This is to ensure that the pre-engagement process should find an appropriate
balance between the SOs’ workload and providing adequate feedback to the applicant.
As required under this decision, data centre applications will be required to provide both
dispatchable and renewable generation. The grid connection for this generation will need to
be applied for via the ECP-GSS application process. The SOs’ connection application
process should outline how the data centre application will interact with their corresponding
generation application(s) in ECP-GSS. Technical specifications and requirements expected
for generation should also be provided to facilitate applicants in their planning.
The CRU requests that, following the publication of this policy decision, each of the electrical
SOs develop and publish an engagement and connection process for data centres in order
to provide transparency and clarity for prospective applicants. This should include a high-
level process timeline to help inform stakeholder engagement expectations. As part of the
development of a connection process based on this decision, the electrical SOs should
outline minimum expected performance and availability requirements for onsite or proximate
generation and/or storage and autoproducer units required through this policy. These
expected performance and availability requirements should acknowledge the need for
routine necessary maintenance on the generation and/or storage assets. It is understood
that the development and publication of the connection engagement and application process
by the SOs will require some time to complete. In order to allow sufficient time to develop
and publish this connection process reflecting this decision the CRU requests that each
electrical SO publishes their respective process by 31 March 2026. Once published new
applicants will then have the transparency and clarity required to advance new data centre
connection applications.

3.9.5. Enforcement
As described above in Section 3.3 Requirements for data centres that have an MIC
<10MVA,  Section 3.4 Requirements for all data centres equal to or above 10 MVA and
Section 3.5 Renewable Electricity Requirement, the CRU’s view is that the energy assets
required under this policy should have to meet the same performance and availability
requirements as any other equivalent unit in the system. This new capacity should be made
available to the system on an operational basis in order to reflect the additional demand
capacity of the data centre and support the continuity, security, and quality of supply of
electricity for the wider system. It is envisaged that reliability of service will be a contractual
requirement in the data centre’s contractual arrangements. If the delivery, performance and
availability of the required energy services falls below this minimum expected reliability or
provision of available capacity to the system, the SOs will have the ability to reduce the MIC
of the related data centres demand connection and/or move it to non-firm status. This should
be set out by the SOs within the contractual arrangements.

3.9.7. Application of this policy to new demand versus increases to existing
demand sites
The CRU notes that some data centre connection applications may relate to existing data

requirements this data centre demand must meet, reflecting the potential different sizes
these MIC increases may represent versus the size of the overall site demand.

The CRU notes concerns raised by the SOs regarding potential behaviour by applicants

4. Gas connections
In Proposed Decision CRU202504 it described how a number of applications from Data
Centres have been received by Gas Networks Ireland (“GNI”) for connection to the gas
system. These connections could be in addition to, or as back-up to, a site’s electrical
connection. Some of these data centre applications may have chosen gas as their primary
source of energy, for example, in cases where they were unable to secure an electrical
connection. In these cases, applicants seek a gas connection to generate electricity onsite
for the data centre load - arrangements known as ‘islanded data centres’ since they are
isolated from the electricity network. It described how the CRU understands that a number of
data centres have been contracted by GNI to connect to the gas system as their primary
energy source.
In the Call for Evidence (CRU/202357) it set out how a coordinated approach for
connections to the electricity and gas networks could ensure that policies introduced for
electricity do not inadvertently result in an unintended consequence of increased
connections to the gas network, and vice-versa. The measures being put in place for the
connection of data centres to the electricity network have been developed in the context of
system constraints and security of supply. Where gas-connected projects are also
connected to the electricity system, these connections can provide resilience for Ireland’s
energy supply. However, the CRU does acknowledge that, due to the scale of these
applicants’ typical energy demands, an influx of a number of these types of users could
impact gas usage and trigger the need for investment in gas infrastructure. It described how
these type of gas users may not represent long term demand (unlike traditional industrial
heat users) and may result in the risk of stranding of gas infrastructure assets as this
demand may seek to electrify in the future.
4.1.1. Security of supply
In Proposed Decision CRU202504  it described how GNI has an obligation under Section
8(2) of the Gas Act 1976 to have regard to the need to ensure the safety and security of the
transmission, distribution and supply of natural gas, and it is essential that GNI continues to
monitor the risk associated with connection applications to the gas network to determine
whether they pose any risk to security of supply or increased network investment costs.

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


93
As set out in Proposed Decision CRU202504, GNI described in the Network Development
Plan 202445 that annual gas demand is expected to increase up to 2025/26 and then decline
for the remaining years of the period towards 2031. Peak day gas demand is predicted to grow
over the ten-year period and is driven by the requirement for dispatchable gas-fired electricity
generation to meet the growing electricity demand on days of low available renewable energy.
The declining long-term trend of emissions intensity of electricity generation and the growing
renewable installed capacity were also described. Some respondents to Proposed Decision
CRU202504 raised concerns that the requirement for data centres to provide onsite or
proximate generation may lead to increased demand on the gas network and result in security
of supply concerns. Some respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 stressed the
importance of a coordinated approach between gas and electricity networks to avoid
unintended consequences, such as increased gas connections due to electricity grid
constraints. Some respondents called for better planning and communication between the
system operators.
4.1.2. Interruptible gas product
The concept of potential future interruptible gas connections was discussed in Consultation
CRU2024001. Proposed Decision CRU202504 described how the Government's Energy
Security in Ireland to 2030 - Energy Security Package (published in November 2023)
outlines that DCEE are leading an action "to review gas connection policy and introduce gas
demand flexibility measures" in 2025. The National Energy Demand Strategy further
reinforces this by assigning an action to GNI to "Undertake assessment to identify flexibility
products & services on the gas network ...". Proposed Decision CRU202504 described how
GNI are working on the development of an interruptible gas capacity product for large energy
users which supports the maintenance of gas supply/demand balance.
Some respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 supported the development of
interruptible gas capacity products for large energy users (LEUs), emphasising their role in
balancing gas supply and demand. Some respondents suggested that such products could
enhance grid stability and provide flexibility for LEUs. Several respondents expressed
concerns about the application of interruptible gas contracts, particularly for projects
providing dispatchable capacity. These respondents argued that reliance on interruptible gas
connections could undermine energy security and operational reliability for data centres.


45 GNI – 2024 – Network Development Plan – link here

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


94
Some respondents suggested the need for clear policies regarding interruptible gas
products. Some respondents suggested that the CRU should provide explicit guidance on
the use of these products and ensure coordination between gas and electricity system
operators to avoid unintended consequences.
4.1.3. Islanded data centres
The July 2022 Government Statement on the Role of Data Centres in Ireland’s Enterprise
Strategy outlined that islanded data centres (i.e. those connected to the gas network but not
the electricity network) would not be in line with national policy, suggesting these would run
counter to emissions reduction objectives and would not serve the wider efficiency and
decarbonisation of the energy system. The Government Statement also said that growth in
‘Islanded’ data centres may transfer security of supply risk from electricity to gas supply,
potentially putting stress on the gas network and gas importation.  In Proposed Decision
CRU202504 it described how the CRU understands that the development of islanded gas
data centres continues not to be in line with Government policy.
Some respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 opposed the development of islanded
data centres, citing concerns about their inconsistency with government policy, their negative
impact on decarbonisation efforts, and their potential to hinder climate goals. Islanded data
centres were described as a step backward in achieving a sustainable energy future. Some
respondents criticised islanded data centres’ reliance on gas connections for exacerbating
dependence on fossil fuels, increasing greenhouse gas emissions, and slowing progress
toward decarbonisation. Some respondents emphasised the need to transition away from
fossil fuels to meet climate objectives.
Some respondents highlighted the lack of clear policy direction and legal basis for
addressing gas connections for islanded data centres. Some respondents called for
coordinated policies between gas and electricity connections and stressed the importance of
aligning with climate action and energy policies. Some respondents discussed the economic
implications of islanded data centres, including the risk of stranded assets, the need for long-
term planning, and the importance of developing a mature renewable gas market.
Some respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 described the use of islanded data
centres as a transitional solution, provided they adhere to strict guidelines and timelines.
Some respondents suggested that these gas connections could be used as a temporary
solution for data centres while waiting for electrical grid connections/upgrade works. Some

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


95
respondents proposed setting a maximum time limit for such interim use to ensure it remains
a short-term (non-enduring) measure.

the gas network, the use of biomethane could play a role in decarbonisation of their demand.
The certainty of long-term contracts with data centres could support the development of

The CRU noted in Proposed Decision CRU202504 the potential role of the gas network in

Some respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 highlighted renewable gases like
biomethane and green hydrogen as essential components in achieving decarbonisation
goals. Some respondents described them as critical for reducing emissions and supporting
Ireland's transition to a sustainable energy system. Some respondents raised concerns
about the limited supply of renewable gases in the medium term and the need for

Some respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 suggested the use of long-term

Some respondents suggested the integration of biomethane and green hydrogen into gas

harder-to-abate sectors rather than for data centres.
4.1.5. Next steps
The CRU is cognisant that there is considerable interaction between the gas and electricity
networks and a coordinated approach to connections to the electricity and gas networks has
merit. The CRU notes the recent update to the Gas Directive (to be transposed by August
2026) states that: "Member States shall endeavour to ensure coordinated planning steps of
the respective ten-year network development plans for natural gas, hydrogen and electricity"
and that this will inform future work in this area. However, the CRU also notes that
coordinated connection policies between gas and electricity for individual connections would
likely require new legislation to be introduced.
The CRU is not proposing to introduce any new decisions relating to connections to the gas
network as part of this review process. The CRU does acknowledge the need to consider
what changes may be required in this regard and is actively engaging with Gas Networks
Ireland to progress the potential introduction of an interruptible gas capacity product and
proposes to consult separately on this topic in the near term.

97
5. Other considerations

This section outlines other issues raised as part of feedback to the proposed decision.

5.1.1. Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA)
The European Directive 2001/42 (the “SEA Directive”) introduces the requirement of Strategic
Environmental Assessment (SEA)47. An SEA is a process for the formal, systematic evaluation
of the likely significant environmental effects of implementing a plan or programme. An SEA
aims to provide for a high level of protection of the environment and to contribute to the
integration of environmental considerations into the preparation and adoption of plans with a
view to promoting sustainable development.
A number of respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 raised the possible need for a
Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) of the CRU’s Review of LEU Connection Policy. It
was suggested that the decision would represent a plan or programme for the energy sector
which sets the framework for data centres and comes within the scope of the SEA Directive.
Therefore, it was suggested that an environmental assessment is required under the SEA
Directive. Another respondent highlighted that the Government Statement on the Role of Data
Centres in Ireland’s Enterprise Strategy, despite being repeatedly utilised as a basis,
framework and justification for further data centre development, was never subject to a SEA.
This respondent suggested that, to their knowledge, no SEA screening was conducted.
The CRU considers that the LEU connection policy, which sets the terms and conditions by
which an individual data centre can connect to the electricity network, does not constitute a
plan or programme for which a requirement for SEA arises under the SEA Directive.

5.1.2. Infrastructure
Some respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 highlighted the need to upgrade
Ireland's electricity grid to accommodate data centre demand while ensuring sustainability.
Some respondents emphasised the need for significant upgrades to Ireland's electricity and
gas infrastructure to support increased electrification and energy demands. The CRU notes

environmental-assessment-sea/

98
the network development plans included in the Price Review 6 (PR6) submissions by the SOs
are developed to deliver upon government and sector plans and policies including renewable
targets, to meet security of supply requirements and to meet the increasing demand for
electricity including for national housing targets. However, in the absence of clarity around the
scale and location of future data centre demand, it is challenging for the system operators to
plan and build the electricity system to meet these potential additional future needs. The CRU
is of the view that a State-led approach to infrastructure development for data centres is
required in order to accommodate such potential future demand.  Such an approach could
encompass spatial planning for data centres, along with targets-based and plan-led
infrastructure development, which drives synergies between energy, environmental and
enterprise policy, and would help to ensure that the utility infrastructure (e.g. energy,
communications, water) required to meet growing demands will be planned in a coordinated
and efficient manner. As described in Proposed Decision CRU202504, in order to better
understand the scale of potential medium-term demand from prospective data centres and to
help inform the potential development of a State-led approach to enable the continued future
development of the data centre sector in Ireland, the CRU requested the electricity and gas
SOs to conduct a market intelligence exercise. Initial feedback from this market intelligence
exercise suggests that there is potential for in the order of 5.8GW additional demand capacity
required for the data centre sector in Ireland in the medium term. This is in addition to demand
already contracted and would require consideration of a bespoke or plan-led approach to
infrastructure development in Ireland.
5.1.3. Private wires
Many respondents suggested private wire systems as a solution to reduce grid strain and
support renewable energy integration. Some respondents recommended implementing private
wire policies, encouraging their use for clean energy, and providing clear guidance on their
role in infrastructure development. In July 2025, DCEE published a Private Wires Policy
Statement48 which states that the Government has decided to allow private wires to be built
and operated in a limited number of circumstances (four use cases were identified) where the
public benefits of allowing such developments are clear. Some of the guiding principles and
objectives for the development of the Private Wires Policy (published in July 2024) were to
accelerate the deployment of renewable generation and storage, and to serve other policy
objectives including security of supply, the offshore wind strategy, the hydrogen strategy,

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


99
industrial policy, and the national climate objective, while not undermining the financing or
efficient development of the National Electricity Grid.
There are a number of complex regulatory and administrative issues that will have to be
addressed prior to the implementation of this policy. This includes a change required to
primary legislation, making detailed regulations and assigning new powers, tasks and
resources to the CRU, and potentially to other bodies. Following the introduction of new
legislation, the CRU will be required to develop and/or update frameworks as required.

5.1.4. Collaboration amongst key stakeholders
Many respondents emphasised the importance of collaboration among stakeholders, and
identified key stakeholders including the CRU (Commission for Regulation of Utilities), EirGrid,
SOs (System Operators), An Coimisiún Pleanála, Planning Authorities, EPA (Environmental
Protection Agency), and Government. These entities were highlighted for their roles in policy
development, implementation, and regulation of data centre connections and energy
infrastructure. The CRU recognises the need for key stakeholders to collaborate in order to
more effectively and efficiently deliver on intended policy outcomes, and considers that
stakeholder collaboration will be required in any potential State-led approach.

5.1.5. Stranded assets
Several respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 highlighted concerns about stranded
assets due to cancelled connection applications, sunk costs, and lack of firm power
availability. It was described that these issues were linked to significant investments in
permitting and site development that remain unutilised, creating uncertainty for developers and
investors. Some respondents raised concerns about the negative message sent to potential
foreign investors due to stranded assets and terminated applications. It was suggested
addressing these issues is seen as critical to maintaining Ireland's reputation as a trustworthy
investment location. Some respondents suggested creating a cross-functional task force to
resolve stranded investment cases, implementing structured dialogue among stakeholders,
and adopting a more dynamic approach to connections to support electrification and reduce
stranded capacity. Some respondents emphasised the importance of distinguishing between
advanced-stage projects with significant investments and speculative projects. It was
suggested that prioritisation should be given to consented more advanced developments to
prevent loss of digital infrastructure and stranded assets.

The requirements in this decision will apply to all new connection applications following the
publication of this decision. Applications that were previously terminated would need to reapply
and be subject to the conditions set out in this new policy.

5.1.6. Cost burden & Tariff review
A number of respondents raised concerns relating to the associated cost impacts on
consumers of requiring new dispatchable generation. It was stated that the consequence of
this may be to increase costs for all consumers. It was suggested that the burden of funding
new generation and/or storage assets as part of this policy would need to be appropriately
shared between the data centre in question, and consumers more broadly. The CRU notes
that all electricity market charges and a significant percentage of electricity network charges
are levied on SEM demand on a €/MWh basis. Any new data centre demand would contribute
towards these costs through their energy payments.
A number of respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 raised the issue of locational
signals for demand customers. These respondents raised the current network tariff structure
and how it does not provide explicit locational signals for demand. These respondents
suggested this should be assessed in the network tariff review to incentivise demand to
locate in the most efficient and/or least constrained areas of the network. The CRU notes
feedback received in relation to the use of the network tariff structure towards providing
explicit locational signals for demand. The CRU has recently re-commenced the Electricity
Network Tariff Structure Review Project49 and stakeholders are invited to engage on this
process as it develops. The CRU notes that additional large demand connections would
increase the charging base for tariffs/charges. This means that the costs captured by the
tariffs/charges are being spread over a larger volume of demand, which has the potential to
lower costs on a per unit basis.

5.1.7. Fault Ride Through
In Proposed Decision CRU202504 the CRU noted the ongoing work in relation to future
standards being developed around system security, including fault ride-through capability. It
was described in Proposed Decision CRU202504 how EirGrid noted in their feedback as

part of this review that operational issues have arisen regarding the technical performance of
data centres on the electricity system. EirGrid’s observations are that the collective response
of data centres to system faults is exacerbating disturbances on the power system via
disconnection and automatic reconnection of their demand, and that this behaviour is
already presenting some technical challenges. In order to alleviate these risks, EirGrid is
engaging with stakeholders in order to develop mandatory Grid Code standards, including
fault ride-through capability, to ensure the SOs can securely accommodate the projected
growth of demand of data centres. Following the introduction of Grid Code standards, it is
expected that similar standards will ultimately be transposed to the Distribution Code.
A number of respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 suggested that flexibility should
be a requirement in the new policy. These respondents suggested that new proven
technologies could be used which deliver real time flexibility to the SO which will eliminate
the risk of fault ride through to the transmission system. One respondent stated that fault ride
through for data centres has emerged as a serious issue and the development of any new
policy cannot ignore this issue. This respondent suggested that the SOs ability to make
further connection offers may be jeopardised unless it can be assured that this issue will not
be factor for any new projects connecting.
The CRU notes that the new Grid Code standards being progressed in relation to Fault Ride
Through are intended to apply to existing and new connections, and consideration should be
given to potential requirements, where known, in the project development stage. The CRU
notes the importance of grid stability to all customers including data centres.

5.1.8. Definition of a data centre
A number of respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 commented on the definition of
a data centre and the need to clarify this. One respondent suggested the definition of a data
centre is too broad, and suggested that the policy should only apply to data centres that
provide cloud services to third parties, or lease space for third party equipment to provide
cloud services, and that operate at scale. Another respondent suggested that the definition
of a data centre as set out should ensure that other LEU types such as dispatchable
demand, electrolysers etc. are not inadvertently captured by this policy. One respondent
stated that it would be important to clarify that the definition of a data centre includes three
key types: hyperscale / wholesale / retail, each with different economic and energy use
profiles. This respondent suggested that Hyperscale and Wholesale data centres are large

energy use facilities, and their energy use is consistent with the description in the policy
paper, but recommended excluding retail data centres (<20MW). The CRU notes feedback
received in relation to the definition of a data centre.

5.1.9. District Heating
A number of respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 supported the use of waste
heat from data centres in local district heating networks. Some respondents were supportive
of district heating as a significant potential contributor to sustainable development in Ireland,
describing the decarbonisation benefits of waste heat generated by data centre facilities
being exported via local district heating schemes serving nearby businesses and/or
residences. One respondent stated that the deployment of district heating networks needs to
be accelerated. One respondent suggested that any requirement for data centres to provide
heat to district heating networks should be voluntary as some locations will suit and some
may not. This respondent stated that the cost of the district heating network cannot be borne
by the heat provider alone.
The CRU understands that Government intends to enact legislation in this area, having
approved the General Scheme of the Heat (Networks and Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill in
November 2024. Enactment will provide the legislative and regulatory framework to support
the development of district heating.  Article 26 (6) of the Energy Efficiency Directive states
that “Member States shall ensure that data centres with a total rated energy input exceeding
1 MW utilise the waste heat or other waste heat recovery applications unless they can show
that it is not technically or economically feasible”. The CRU notes that the policy framework
for district heating networks is evolving, that Government policy supports the expansion of
district heating in Ireland to contribute to the diversification of fuel supply and
decarbonisation of the heat sector, and the allocation of funding by Government from the
Climate Action Fund in July 2025 to support pre-construction development costs for efficient
district heating projects in Ireland. The CRU does not intend to create a mandate relating to
district heating for data centre requirements as part of this decision.

5.1.10. Energy Efficiency Directive
A respondent to Proposed Decision CRU202504 highlighted the requirement under the
Energy Efficiency Directive for EU Member States to reduce their energy consumption, and

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities

considers that the CRU should (at least) indicate that data centre growth in Ireland presents
a risk to meeting this requirement.
Article 4 of the Energy Efficiency Directive sets a target for reducing the Final Energy
Consumption of EU Member States by 2030 by 11.7% compared to 2020. The individual
contributions from each Member State were to be determined as set out in the Directive as
part of the development of their National Energy and Climate Plans. Ireland’s indicative
target was approved in February 2024 as 10.451 Mtoe of Final Energy Consumption, a
reduction of 12.6% on the 11.969 Mtoe consumed in 2022. Ireland’s National Energy and
Climate Plan50 acknowledges the significant challenge that this presents and that energy
consumption is likely to rise in the short term, but that alongside existing policies and
measures in place, further initiatives are intended to be developed to meet the target.

6. Direction to System Operators

Upon publication of this Large Energy Users connection policy decision, direction CRU/21/124
will be superseded by the new direction to the SOs as set out in this Section 6.2 below.
6.1. Previous 2021 direction in relation to data centres
As described in Proposed Decision CRU202504 following extensive engagement between the
CRU and EirGrid on security of supply matters and the role of data centres in this context,
EirGrid sent a letter to CRU dated 27 May 2021, which outlined their concerns. In response to
this in June 2021 the CRU published a consultation paper (CRU/21/060). This was in the
context of a wider system security review, including greater insight into the delivery of
generation through the Capacity Remuneration Mechanism pipeline, short-term security of
supply challenges and network constraints. It was clear that measures would need to be
implemented in order to prevent new connections for data centres from exacerbating some of
these risks.
The CRU identified risks that continuing to allow data centres to connect to the electricity
network in accordance with previously established arrangements would have significantly
impacted the CRU’s ability to comply with its statutory obligation to protect the security of
supply of electricity by ensuring that electricity system can meet the reasonable demands of
all consumers, including the demands of existing data centres. Following a consultation
process, in November 2021, the CRU issued directions to the Electricity TSO, EirGrid, and
the Distribution System Operator (Electricity DSO), ESB Networks, regarding the
assessment of data centre connection applications (CRU/21/124). This was in response to
an evolving, significant risk to electricity security of supply in Ireland, and network constraints
identified by the SOs.
6.1.1. Assessment Criteria (CRU/21/124) - 2021 direction
The 2021 direction text stated: “Pursuant to Section 34(1) of the Electricity Regulation Act
1999 (the Act), the CRU directs EirGrid as (TSO) & ESBN as (DSO) to assess applications for
the connection of data centres by reference to the following assessment criteria to determine
whether a connection offer can be made within the system stability and reliability needs of the
electricity network:
•
The location of the data centre applicant with respect to whether they are within a
constrained or unconstrained region of the electricity system.

The ability of the data centre applicant to bring onsite dispatchable generation (and/or

6.1.2. Proposed Direction text outlined in Proposed Decision CRU202504
In Proposed Decision CRU202504 the CRU set out proposed text to replace direction criteria
in the 2021 direction. This proposed to direct the electrical SOs (EirGrid and ESB Networks) to
assess applications for the connection of data centres by reference to the following
assessment criteria to determine whether a connection offer can be made within the system
stability and reliability needs of the electricity network:
•
The location of the data centre applicant with respect to whether they are within a
constrained or unconstrained region of the electricity system.
•
The ability of the data centre applicant to bring onsite or proximate dispatchable
generation (and/or storage) capacity equivalent to or greater than their demand, that

relevant SO, in order to support security of supply.
•
The ability of the data centre applicant to bring demand flexibility provisions if deemed
necessary by the relevant SO.
•
The applicant’s commitment to self-report to SOs on the data centre site’s emissions
and use of renewable energy on an annual basis.

6.2. New direction in relation to data centres

connected and metered, which meets appropriate availability and other technical
requirements as may be specified by the relevant SO, in order to support security of
supply.
•
For data centre applicants with an MIC equal to or above the de-minimis level, the
ability of the data centre applicant to meet at least 80% of their annual demand through

7. Future potential evolution of LEU policy

As described in Proposed Decision CRU202504 there are a number of areas where
developments may occur in the coming years that may provide more opportunities to further
develop the connection policy for LEUs. In particular, the CRU will review the connection
policy as government policy continues to evolve and as markets emerge for the provision of
flexibility products. Some of the relevant areas are set out in detail below.

7.1.1. Data Centre market intelligence exercise
As described in Proposed Decision CRU202504 in order to better understand the scale of
potential medium-term demand from prospective data centres and to help inform the
potential development of a State-led approach to enable the continued future development
of the data centre sector in Ireland, the CRU requested the electricity and gas SOs to
conduct a market intelligence exercise. The data and analysis provided to CRU may be used
to inform future policy development, e.g. a potential State-led strategic approach to delivery
of utility infrastructure for data centres in the medium term, and to highlight any risks arising
in relation to accommodating organic economic growth. This work is being carried out in
parallel with this ongoing review and will be focussed on informing the medium-term
approach. Initial feedback from this market intelligence exercise suggests that there is
potential for in the order of 5.8GW additional demand capacity required for the data centre
sector in Ireland in the medium term. This is in addition to demand already contracted and
would require consideration of a bespoke or plan-led approach to infrastructure development
in Ireland.

7.1.2. State-led approach
The Government Statement on the Role of Data Centres in Ireland’s Enterprise Strategy51
published in July 2022 set out the Government policy aims of enabling the “twin transitions”
of digitalisation and decarbonisation of our economy and society, recognising the value of
renewable energy and digital technologies to Ireland.

In Proposed Decision CRU202504 it described how, in light of Government policy to support
the “twin transitions” of digitalisation and decarbonisation of our economy and society, and
the scale of data centre demand growth relative to the size of Ireland’s electricity system, the
CRU is of the view that the step-change in energy requirements from LEUs requires a
strategic approach to infrastructure development. It was described that, while this connection
policy seeks to provide clarity on the pathway to connections in the near term, a longer-term
approach is required to provide clear investment signals.
Initial feedback from the data centre market intelligence exercise performed by the system
operators exercise suggests that there is potential for in the order of 5.8GW additional
demand capacity required for the data centre sector in Ireland in the medium term. This is in
addition to demand already contracted. The CRU is of the view that the scale of potential
LEU development requires a longer-term State-led approach encompassing spatial planning
for data centres, along with targets-based and plan-led infrastructure development, which
drives synergies between energy, environmental and enterprise policy. This will help to
ensure that the utility infrastructure (e.g. energy, communications, water etc.) required to
meet growing demands will be planned in a coordinated and efficient manner, and will
provide certainty to the investment community in relation to planning of future projects. As
part of this approach consideration should be given to the associated costs and benefits, and
any potential risks arising from high volumes of similar demand customer types.
In Proposed Decision CRU202504 it described how as part of the National Energy Demand
Strategy (NEDS) decision52, the CRU outlined one of the key recommendations for
Government Departments, particularly DCEE and DETE, to support the implementation of the
NEDS as follows:
1. Consider a national strategic approach for the facilitation of new LEU connections
Consideration to be given to a national strategic approach for the planning of large
demand customers and associated infrastructure requirements (e.g. energy, water,
broadband, transport etc.), the associated costs and benefits, and any potential risks
arising from high volumes of similar demand customer types.
Some respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 emphasised the importance of a
State-led approach to energy policy development, advocating for structured guidance and
coordination across government departments and agencies. This approach was seen by

respondents as essential for ensuring successful implementation of policies and
infrastructure development. Some respondents described a State-led approach as a means
to bring together industry stakeholders, public agencies, and private entities to achieve
holistic and efficient policy implementation. The State-led approach was described as
requiring strategic infrastructure and spatial planning, and aiming to improve coordination,
reduce delays, and support the transition to net-zero energy systems. This includes aligning
energy generation, consumption, and spatial policies. It was described that while a State-led
approach provides structured guidance, concerns were raised about the potential rigidity of
this approach and the risk of stifling innovation. The key recommendations arising from the
feedback to Proposed Decision CRU202504 are that a State-led approach should:
•
Clarify leadership and oversight: Establish which department or public authority will
coordinate a State-led approach, ensuring a clear mandate and streamlined decision-
making processes.
•
Confirm legal basis and regulatory scope: Address questions regarding statutory
powers, particularly in relation to Section 15(1) of the Climate Act.
•
Promote cross-Governmental coordination: Ensure alignment between relevant
departments and agencies to support coherent policy implementation and avoid
fragmentation.
•
Integrate spatial and infrastructure planning: Align land-use, zoning, and
development strategies to support the effective rollout of priority infrastructure.
•
Balance strategic certainty with operational flexibility: Design the approach to provide
clear long-term direction while allowing for responsiveness to evolving technologies,
demand patterns, and market conditions.
In the CRU’s view a strategic State-led approach to economic development and coordinated
infrastructure delivery can address some of the challenges being faced in terms of grid
capacity and security of supply in the medium to long term.

7.1.3. Renewable generation
Proposed Decision CRU202504 described how Ireland has significant renewable energy
potential with a non-binding target of up to 37GW of offshore wind, 12GW of onshore wind53
and up to 12GW of utility scale solar PV to be developed by 2050. Respondents to Proposed

Decision CRU202504 cited the potential role of data centres in supporting decarbonisation.
Many respondents emphasised the importance of integrating data centres with renewable
energy sources. Many respondents emphasised the importance of co-locating data centres
with renewable energy sources to enhance efficiency and reduce costs. Suggestions included
encouraging data centres to invest in renewable energy, storage, and energy efficiency.
Some respondents to Proposed Decision CRU202504 favoured evolving policies to adapt to
technological advancements and market needs. The need for clear pathways to achieve net-
zero emissions, including the adoption of renewable energy technologies, performance-based
incentives, and strategic planning for energy transition was highlighted. Some respondents
raised concerns about the lack of a comprehensive energy transition masterplan and the need
for clarity in policy timelines, with many suggesting collaboration among planning agencies

decision to require data centres to meet at least 80% of their annual demand with additional
renewable energy generated in the Republic of Ireland. This level is based on national

could be facilitated via CPPA or directly developed renewable assets. This will help ensure
additionality of renewables e.g. renewable energy projects not facilitated through RESS. The
CRU may review these renewable energy requirements in the future based on developments
such as changed national renewable energy targets.
In Call for Evidence CRU202357 and Consultation CRU2024001 the CRU described the
potential use of timestamped Guarantees of Origin (GOs) and/or renewable credits towards
facilitating meeting possible future real-time zero emission requirements. It was described how
there is ongoing work being carried out in this area. Previous feedback referenced the

Action Plan that sets out that SEAI /CRU /EirGrid /ESBN are to deliver the ‘Implementation of
enhanced emissions reporting framework for electricity emissions for large energy users and
the system operators dispatch actions’. As part of this action, SEAI published the ‘LEU

7.1.4. Generation Adequacy
As outlined in Proposed Decision CRU202504 Ireland has significant targets for renewable
generation which exceed current projections for electricity demand. As these projects are built
out, along with the development of the electricity grid and other capacity procured through
auction processes, the requirements as deemed necessary for new data centre connections in
this policy decision may be reviewed. EirGrid will continue to monitor the adequacy of the
electricity system. The requirements associated with generation adequacy set out in this policy
may also be reviewed in the future. Consideration may also have to be given to the interaction
if any, with  any potential future State-led approach for the development of data centres in
Ireland.

7.1.5. Additional flexibility products and markets
As described in Proposed Decision CRU202504 and Section 3.7 above, the development of
further flexibility products and markets can help unlock the flexibility potential of LEU
demand while at the same time providing beneficial revenue returns. Some respondents to
Proposed Decision CRU202504 emphasised the importance of making demand flexibility a
mandatory requirement in new policies. Other respondents suggested that flexibility should
be incentivised through market mechanisms rather than imposed as a penalty/requirement.
Some respondents cited benefits of demand flexibility such as enhanced system efficiency,
reduce carbon emissions, and optimised renewable energy usage.
As further developments emerge in the area of demand flexibility, and as the SO systems
and controls evolve, the CRU may review the need for mandatory flexibility provisions in
future.

7.1.6. Connection charging
As the profile of demand customers changes, there may be benefit to carrying out a review of
connection charging policy to ensure an appropriate balance can continue to be struck
between upfront connections costs and charges & tariffs paid over the lifetime of the
connection.

8. Next steps
Decision and SO direction
This paper sets out the CRU’s decision in relation to the new LEU connection policy. These
decisions will apply to all new connection applications for new or additional capacity
captured under the scope of the decision. Direction CRU/21/124 is now superseded by this
new direction to the SOs. The SOs will update the relevant policies and processes required
for implementation of this decision.
SO connection process
The SOs will publish an engagement and connection process for data centre connection
applicants based on this decision by 31 March 2026. Once published new applicants will then
have the transparency and clarity required to advance new possible data centre connection
applications.
Publication of network information
Following on from this consultation, the Commission requires the SOs to publish regular up
to date locational information (existing and outlook) in relation to the availability of capacity
on the electricity network and network constraint. The SOs are to provide initial proposals in
relation to these requirements, including how to capture interaction between the
transmission and distribution systems, by 31 March 2026.
Gas
The CRU is not proposing to introduce any new decisions relating to connections to the gas
network as part of this review process. However, the CRU does acknowledge the need to
consider what changes may be required in this regard and is actively engaging with Gas
Networks Ireland to progress the potential introduction of an interruptible gas capacity
product and proposes to consult separately on this topic in the near term.
Medium term
In the CRU’s view a strategic State-led approach to economic development and coordinated
infrastructure delivery can address some of the challenges being faced in terms of grid
capacity and security of supply in the medium to long term. The CRU will work with the
relevant Government departments and agencies to support any such developments in this
area.

The following section provides a high-level summary of some of the key messages received
through feedback to each question of proposed decision CRU202504.

The CRU has fully considered all submissions made in response to Proposed Decision
CRU/202504 as part of the process of setting the connection policy set out in this Decision
Paper. While it is not possible to include every detail of each submission given the detailed
nature of many of the submissions received, this summary is provided by way of assistance
to readers.

Q1. Comments are invited from interested parties in relation to the topics covered in
Section 2 Constrained regions of the electrical system and security of supply.
Many respondents discussed the significant challenges posed by network constraints,
particularly in the Greater Dublin Area. It was described how these constraints affect grid
capacity, security of supply, and the ability to accommodate new connections, including data
centres. It was described that the Greater Dublin Area, including counties Dublin, Meath, and
Kildare, were identified as a Tier 1 location for data centre connectivity. However, significant
network constraints exist, requiring detailed maps, timelines for grid investments, and
strategic planning to address these issues effectively.
In response to these challenges some respondents suggested publishing detailed maps of
constrained areas, conducting cost-benefit analyses, and implementing measures such as
self-generation, storage, and flexible resources to alleviate congestion. Some respondents
also proposed self-generation capabilities, battery energy storage systems, and generation
fuelled by hydrogen to transform data centres into active contributors to grid stability.
Stakeholders emphasised the need for transparency and flexibility in planning and decision-
making.
Stakeholders highlighted the need for a State-led strategic approach to address the
challenges of data centre growth. It was indicated that this approach would balance
economic benefits with infrastructure upgrades and ensure alignment with national policy
objectives. Stakeholders stressed the importance of coordinated energy policies across
government departments. There was strong support from some respondents for conducting

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


116
a market intelligence exercise to gather data on electricity and gas demand from data
centres. Stakeholders emphasize the importance of publishing anonymised findings from the
market intelligence exercise to inform future policy and planning.
Data centres were identified by some respondents as major contributors to electricity
demand and network constraints. It was described how rapid growth in data centres is
surpassing the pace of grid infrastructure development, creating pressures on the network.
Concerns were raised about the impact of unconstrained growth on infrastructure, resilience,
and investor confidence. Some stakeholders recommend prioritising security of supply and
integrating renewable energy solutions to support sustainable growth.  Some respondents
described the economic benefits of data centres, foreign direct investment, and the need for
clear, stable, and predictable energy policies. Some respondents described that balancing
economic growth with sustainability and security of supply is essential.
Some respondents discussed the impact of data centres on CO2 emissions, decarbonisation
targets, and the importance of sustainable development. Recommendations included
prioritising projects that contribute to GHG emissions savings and transitioning data centres
into contributors to grid stability and sustainability.
Some respondents called for increased transparency in planning and consultation
processes, publishing findings of market intelligence exercises, and engaging stakeholders
to address challenges effectively. Suggestions include clarifying definitions and timelines for
grid investments. Some respondents underscored the importance of clear and predictable
energy policies to support future development of data centres and other large energy users.
It was suggested that these policies should ensure sustainable growth, avoid retroactive
measures, and foster innovation while addressing network constraints and achieving climate
targets.

Q2. Comments are invited from interested parties in relation to the topics described in
Section 3 Proposed decision on electricity connections.
The below text summarises some of the key themes discussed by respondents.

Who policy applies to

117
In terms of who the policy should apply to, some respondents emphasised the need for clear
definitions and classifications of data centres and LEUs. A number of respondents agreed
with the proposed approach of this policy applying exclusively to data centres. It was stated
that this is justified given the relatively small size of the SEM, and the growing proportion of
total electricity demand utilised by data centres. It was also highlighted that it is important
that the beneficial role data centres can play the electricity system as a whole is recognised.
It was described by one respondent that they recognise the impact that data centres have on
a grid such as Ireland’s, but any targeted policy should only apply over a certain MIC. While
another respondent stated policy should apply to all data centres regardless of size and
without a de minimis level being introduced. Some respondents proposed distinguishing
between hyperscale, wholesale, and retail data centres, and ensuring policies do not
inadvertently affect other LEU types like biomethane plants. It was described that hyperscale
self-build represents three-quarters of the existing data centre footprint in Ireland, with over
half of Ireland’s operational data centres below 10 MW IT capacity. It was stated these data
centres have less than 18% of the total MIC power capacity of all operational data centres in
Ireland, with data centres above 10 MW IT having 82% of the MIC capacity. Some
respondents discussed including minimum connection thresholds, setting thresholds for MIC
and energy usage, and clarifying policies for different types of data centres. Some
respondents raised concerns about policies targeting data centres exclusively, with
suggestions that this policy should apply to all LEUs. These respondents highlighted the
importance of non-discrimination and the need for balanced approaches to energy
consumption and decarbonisation goals. Some respondents called for regulatory clarity on
connection policies, thresholds, and their application to existing and new facilities.

Proximate generation
Many respondents emphasised the need for a clear and precise definition of the term
'proximate generation'. Suggestions include defining it as either geographically or electrically
proximate, with some advocating for a radius-based or substation-based approach.
Suggestions include defining it as assets connected at the same electrical node or within a
specific radius, and clarifying its implications for grid stability and planning. It was suggested
that the lack of clarity had caused confusion among stakeholders. Some respondents
expressed concerns about the feasibility of meeting proximate generation requirements due
to planning, financial, and logistical challenges. The economic and operational challenges of
implementing proximate generation were discussed, some respondents cited issues like the

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


118
complexity of SEM participation, the economic viability of small-scale generation, and the
burden on data centres to construct generation facilities. Some respondents suggested
incorporating renewable energy and storage solutions into proximate generation to enhance
sustainability and decarbonisation.

Derating factors
Many respondents expressed concerns about the application of de-rating factors to
generation and storage. Some respondents argued that de-rating factors can change over
time, creating uncertainty for planning and investment. Some respondents suggested fixing
de-rating factors before planning to ensure proper sizing of generation and demand load.
Many respondents stated that current de-rating levels for storage are too low, making it
economically unviable. Some respondents suggested applying more favourable de-rating
factors for storage to encourage participation in the market. Some respondents highlighted
that de-rating factors influence the economic feasibility of participating in the Single
Electricity Market (SEM). They argue that overly stringent de-rating requirements could deter
investment in renewable and storage technologies, potentially undermining the goals of
decarbonisation and energy security. Some respondents proposed up-rating factors for
storage or reducing the de-rating requirements for renewable generation outside of support
schemes. Some respondents suggested that de-rating factors should account for the
performance and availability of generation without imposing stricter requirements. Some
respondents requested more detail on how de-rating factors will be applied, particularly for
new technologies like Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), emphasising the importance
of transparency to avoid unintended market distortions.

Participation in the SEM
Some stakeholders expressed concerns about the requirement for data centres to
participate in the SEM. Some respondents suggested that SEM participation introduces
significant financial and logistical burdens, potentially undermining the business case for
data centres. Concerns included the need for major capital expenditures and the risk of
unintended consequences in the market. Some respondents argued that mandatory
participation may render projects commercially unviable and misaligned with long-term
energy strategies. Some respondents suggested allowing non-market-integrated on-site

An Coimisiún um Rialáil Fóntais Commission for Regulation of Utilities


119
generation, to reduce barriers while ensuring system flexibility and reliability. In relation to
the capacity market, some respondents expressed concerns about the mandatory
requirement for data centres to participate in the CRM, citing increased complexity, cost, and
planning challenges. Some respondents suggested that this requirement may deter
investment and proposed alternative approaches to ensure flexibility and reduce burdens.
Some respondents emphasised the need for clarity on how CRM participation integrates with
planning frameworks, grid codes, and regulatory processes. Some respondents requested
detailed guidance on ramping requirements, capacity allocation, and the impact on the
demand curve. Some respondents sought clarity on the effect the entry of new demand may
have on the capacity auction demand curve.

New generation
A number of respondents emphasised the need for explicit definitions and clarity regarding
what constitutes 'new generation.' Some respondents requested that the policy explicitly
state whether new generation is required and how it will be defined, including its eligibility for
capacity auctions and contracts. Some respondents expressed concerns about the
economic feasibility of requiring new generation. They highlight issues such as high capital
expenditure, planning complexities, and the potential for making data centre projects
commercially unviable.

Ramping/timing requirements
Some respondents raised concerns about the practicality of ramping requirements, including
the need for significant capital investment and the lack of clear guidance on ramp rates,
intervals, and milestones. It was suggested that ramping requirements may lead to
oversupply of gas-fired generation and pose operational challenges. Some respondents
suggested replacing linear ramp-up provisions with milestone-based approaches tied to grid
connection and system needs. Some respondents proposed allowing phased compliance to
align generation capacity with operational scale-up. Ramping requirements were seen as
adding complexity, time, and cost to data centre developments. Some respondents
emphasised the importance of clear definitions for ramping requirements, with clarity needed
to ensure alignment with market and regulatory frameworks.

Separate connections
A number of respondents support the requirement for onsite/proximate generation to be
independently connected to the grid rather than directly to the data centre. This approach is
seen as beneficial for ensuring system reliability and optimising the use of dispatchable
energy plants. However, some respondents raised concerns about the practicality and
economic viability of separate connections for onsite/proximate generation. Issues raised
include increased complexity, cost, and planning challenges, as well as the potential for
inefficiencies in the system. One respondent highlighted the need for significant
infrastructure investment due to the requirement for a separate grid connection for each
generator, resulting in increased capital expenditure for data centres and grid operators. It
was described how this setup introduces inefficiencies in energy use, as power generated
on-site must first be exported to the grid before it can be consumed by the data centre,
causing an unnecessary transmission and/or distribution loss. This respondent suggested
that a more technically and economically efficient approach would be to integrate onsite
generation directly with LEU demand. Some respondents requested clearer definitions and
guidelines for separate connections, including what constitutes 'proximate' generation and
how these connections will be implemented in practice. Stakeholders emphasised the need
for detailed rulesets and regulatory clarity to avoid misinterpretation and ensure effective
implementation. There were concerns about the economic and operational implications for
data centres, particularly regarding market integration and compliance requirements.

Reliability and performance of generation assets
A number of respondents provided feedback about the reliability of generation assets,
including the need for clear performance criteria, maintenance standards, and the ability to
meet demand during outages. Some respondents emphasised how reliability is critical for
ensuring uninterrupted operations and meeting system requirements. Some respondents
noted that it is in the interest of large energy users to maintain their systems to ensure
consistent performance and availability of the related generation. Concerns were raised
about the impact of outages and run-hour limitations. Some respondents requested clarity on
performance metrics, it was suggested these metrics are critical for planning and investment
decisions and ensuring generation assets meet operational needs. It was suggested that de-
